b.bio: John of Garland was an English grammarian, lexicographer, and poet who spent most of his life in France. He was born in England and studied at Oxford before going to Paris in 1202 to complete his studies; he taught there from about 1220, living on the Left Bank at the Clos de Garlande. In 1229 he joined the new University of Toulouse as one of its first masters, fleeing the city around 1232–1233 when Cathar influence returned after the Albigensian Crusade, escaping disguised as a serf. Back in Paris by 1234, he wrote verse treatises on accentuation (Accentuarium) and the liturgy (Carmen de Ecclesia, dedicated to Fulk, Bishop of London), and the epic De triumphis ecclesiae, finished in 1252.
b.s: The works held here show both sides of his output: pedagogical word-books (synonyms, equivocal terms, orthography) that shaped medieval Latin study, and an allegorical fragment reading the Church as a house built on Christ the rock with the saints carried by him to heaven.

b.bio: The author is an English Puritan preacher named John Rogers whose treatises on faith, watchfulness, love, and his exposition of 1 Peter were printed between 1618 and 1650. He must not be confused with the earlier John Rogers (c. 1500/1505–1555), Bible editor and Protestant martyr under Mary I, who died decades before any of these works appeared. No surviving record gives dates or offices for this later Rogers.
b.s: The works here are practical Puritan divinity: an expository commentary on 1 Peter and treatises on faith, sanctification, love, and Christian watchfulness. They argue that faith in God's promise sustains believers in affliction, that love is the fulfilling of the law, and that unbelief is the root of all sin, written largely against Popery and for the assurance of believers.

b.bio: Jean Garnier was a French Jesuit patristic scholar, theologian, and historian. Entering the Society of Jesus in 1628, he taught humanities, philosophy, and theology at various colleges, notably the Collège de Clermont in Paris. He was widely recognized for his vast erudition in early church history, canon law, and patristics, producing critical editions and extensive historical dissertations.
b.s: He is best remembered for his major scholarly editions of fifth-century patristic texts and the ancient papal chancery formulary, the Liber Diurnus.

b.bio: Jean La Placette (1629-1718) was a French Reformed (Huguenot) pastor and moral theologian who, after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes, led the French Protestant congregation at Copenhagen under royal favor. A prolific controversialist, he wrote extensively on conscience, casuistry, and free will, disputing with Pierre Bayle over faith and reason and defending human liberty against strict predestinarian critics such as Philippe Naudé. His works on moral liberty and physical premotion are important documents of the Huguenot diaspora's engagement with early Enlightenment skepticism.

b.bio: John Smith was born at Lowther, Westmorland on 10 November 1659, one of eleven brothers. He studied at St John's College, Cambridge (B.A. 1677, M.A. 1681), was ordained by Archbishop Sterne, and became a minor canon of Durham Cathedral in 1682, later chaplain to Lord Lansdown at Madrid (1686–89). Bishop Nathaniel Crew collated him to Gateshead rectory in 1695 and to a prebendal stall at Durham; he became D.D. at Cambridge in 1696 and treasurer of Durham in 1699, adding the rectory of Bishop-Wearmouth in 1704. His health failed from 1713 and he died in 1715.
b.s: He is remembered for his edition of Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum; the works held here are his annotations on Bede's texts, in which he defends Bede against the criticisms of Oxford scholars and Stillingfleet, drawing on Camden, Nennius, Gildas, Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory of Tours.

He studied at St John's College, Cambridge (B.A. 1677, M.A. 1681), was ordained by Archbishop Sterne, and became a minor canon of Durham Cathedral in 1682, later chaplain to Lord Lansdown at Madrid (1686–89). Bishop Nathaniel Crew collated him to Gateshead rectory in 1695 and to a prebendal stall at Durham; he became D.D. at Cambridge in 1696 and treasurer of Durham in 1699, adding the rectory of Bishop-Wearmouth in 1704. His health failed from 1713 and he died in 1715.
b.s: He is remembered for his edition of Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum; the works held here are his annotations on Bede's texts, in which he defends Bede against the criticisms of Oxford scholars and Stillingfleet, drawing on Camden, Nennius, Gildas, Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory of Tours.

b.bio: The works held under this name are those of a Roman Catholic controversialist writing between 1626 and 1678. The record's theses — episcopal succession as the mark of the true church, the mass as a propitiatory sacrifice, invocation of saints, and sustained attacks on Protestants, Luther, and Calvin — place this author firmly on the Catholic side of the English polemical literature. No surviving record gives his biography or dates.
b.s: His works here form a substantial Catholic counter-attack on Protestant claims about church, worship, and scriptural interpretation, arguing antiquity and episcopal succession against Luther, Calvin, and the Protestants generally, while citing authorities such as Augustine and Jewel.

b.bio: Surviving records do not clearly identify this author: they cover a later Trinity controversialist (1686–1763) and a nineteenth-century bishop, neither of whom matches the library's holdings. The works held under this name — sermons and treatises printed between 1628 and 1668, arguing against Quakers (including James Naylor), Seekers, and Papists — belong to an earlier English divine for whom these sources give no dates or biography. He wrote on conscience, the eternity of mankind's future state, the restoration of true ministry after discontinuance, and compiled an Index Biblicus concordance.
b.s: His works here are anti-Quaker polemic and practical divinity from the Interregnum, including responses to Naylor and the Seekers and a treatise defending the eternity of future punishment.

b.bio: the surviving records describe a different man of the same name: John Stoughton (1807–1897), the Norwich-born Congregational minister and historical theologian, author of an Ecclesiastical History of England. He cannot be the author of A Forme of Wholsome Words, printed in 1640, decades before his birth. The library's volume belongs to an earlier John Stoughton whose works circulated in print in 1640; no source in this record gives his dates or offices, so none are asserted here.
b.s: A Forme of Wholsome Words (1640) builds divinity on 'sound words' of Scripture, treating prolegomena and theological method, the church as typified by the material temple, every member's useful service according to differing abilities, and the one needful good above worldly distractions.

b.bio: the surviving records describe three other men named John Ward: a Gresham College professor of rhetoric (c. 1679–1758), a Dean of Lincoln (1779–1860), and the Royalist vicar of Stratford-upon-Avon (1629–1681) who kept a diary. None is this author, so none of their details are used here. The John Ward held in this collection preached before the Honourable House of Commons in 1645 and published Parliamentarian sermons and tracts between 1642 and 1645; no source in hand gives his dates or offices, so none are asserted.
b.s: His five works here are Civil War pulpit polemic: sermons to Parliament on God judging among the gods and on providence, a tract arguing the lawfulness of Parliament's war against the bishops' 'Bellum Episcopale', an exhortation to contend for gospel and Christian liberty against prelates and Rome, and a news-account of the taking of Winchester.

b.bio: the surviving records describe three unrelated men named John Williams: a contemporary Church of England lecturer at York St John, a Welsh-born Baptist missionary (1767–1825), and the antiquary John Williams (Ab Ithel, 1811–1862). None of them matches this author, so none of the source material is used here. The library's record shows an early-seventeenth-century English divine whose printed works run from 1620 to 1672: defences of the communion table against the name 'altar', a sermon and treatise on Solomon as a type of King James, a Latin case for perseverance, and papers from 1641–1642 defending the twelve bishops against impeachment. No source gives his dates or offices, so none is asserted here.
b.s: His works here defend the Church of England as a true church separated from Rome, argue that the Lord's Supper utensil is a table not an altar, and document the episcopal defence at the outbreak of the Civil War.

b.bio: Joseph Saenz de Aguirre was a Spanish Benedictine of the Monte Cassino congregation, born at Logroño in Old Castile on 24 March 1630. He directed studies at the Monastery of St. Vincent of Salamanca for fifteen years and became its abbot, then taught dogmatic theology and inaugurated a course in Holy Scripture at the University of Salamanca. He served as councillor and secretary of the Holy Office and president of its Spanish congregation. His work against the Declaration of the Gallican Clergy of 1682 earned him a cardinal's hat from Innocent XI in 1686, and his correspondence with Bossuet shows his opposition to Quietism. He died in Rome on 19 August 1699.
b.s: The works held here are historical notices printed in PL 80, where Aguirre appears as an editor of patristic material rather than as an ancient author.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies who 'J. Albani' was. The single work held here is a two-page Latin piece from Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 185 recording the extension to Bernard of Clairvaux of the title Doctor of the Church by Pius VIII in 1830, answering objections raised by the Promoter of the Faith and citing curial figures of that era (Cardinal Zurla, Giulio Maria de Somalia). the surviving records describe Gian Girolamo Albani (1509–1591), cardinal and jurist of Bergamo, author of legal-ecclesiastical treatises such as De Donatione Constantini — a different person, and no source links him to this document.
b.s: The work held here is a brief curial record of Bernard of Clairvaux's proclamation as Doctor of the universal Church, with the objections against it answered and a plenary indulgence attached to its commemoration.

w: Second Table in the Commentaries on the Song of Songs
Table in the Commentaries on the Song of Songs

b.bio: Jodocus Badius, called Ascensius from his birthplace Asse near Brussels, was born in 1462 and died in 1535. Educated by the Brethren of the Common Life at Ghent, he studied at Brussels and Ferrara, taught Greek at Lyon, and worked there as proofreader and editor for the printer Johann Trechsel from 1492 to 1498. In 1503 he established his own press in Paris, the Prelum Ascensianum, which produced some 775 editions over three decades, chiefly Latin classical texts with his own student commentaries, alongside grammatical, moral, philosophical and theological works. He was associated with humanists including Robert Gaguin, Lefèvre d'Étaples, Guillaume Budé and Erasmus.
b.s: The works held here are not treatises but two reference tables (8 pages total) appended to commentaries on the Song of Songs printed in PL 206; they index that text, citing among others Thomas, monk of Cîteaux, and John Algrin of Abbeville.

w: Notice of the manuscripts of Lactantius from the Vatican

b.bio: Born in Hasroun, Mount Lebanon (North Lebanon), into a Maronite family of scholars, Assemani was educated at the Maronite College in Rome and then worked at the Vatican Library as scribe and translator, cataloguing manuscripts brought from Egypt in 1707 by his relative Elias. He travelled twice to the Middle East (1715–17 and 1735–38) acquiring manuscripts for the Vatican. In 1739 he was appointed First Custodian of the Vatican Library; in 1766 he became titular Archbishop of Tyre. His Bibliotheca Orientalis Clementino-Vaticana was the first European history of Syriac literature.
b.s: The work held here is a two-page notice on the manuscripts of Lactantius preserved in the Vatican, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 6) as a scholarly apparatus to the Lactantius volume.

b.bio: Jacques Basnage de Beauval was born at Rouen in 1653, son of the lawyer Henri Basnage de Franquesnay. He studied classical languages at Saumur and theology at Geneva, and was pastor at Rouen from 1676 until the revocation of the Edict of Nantes forced him to Holland in 1685. He settled in Rotterdam as a minister pensionary until 1691, when he became pastor of the Walloon church of Rotterdam; in 1709 grand pensionary Heinsius secured his election as one of the pastors of the Walloon church at The Hague, intending to employ him mainly in civil affairs, including a secret negotiation with Marshal d'Uxelles, French plenipotentiary at the congress of Utrecht. He wrote a history of the Reformed churches and on Jewish antiquities, and is especially remembered for his debate with Bossuet.
b.s: The pieces held here are his critical apparatus printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina: notes and observations defending the authenticity of texts such as Faustus of Riez's letter to Leontius and Lucidus's letter and abjuration, taking a middle position between Sirmundus and Mauguinus on Faustus's doctrine of grace and opposing Baronius.

b.bio:
Jacques Basnage (1653–1723) — Jacques Basnage de Beauval was born at Rouen in 1653, son of the lawyer Henri Basnage de Franquesnay. He studied classical languages at Saumur and theology at Geneva, and was pastor at Rouen from 1676 until the revocation of the Edict of Nantes forced him to Holland in 1685. He settled in Rotterdam as a minister pensionary until 1691, when he became pastor of the Walloon church of Rotterdam; in 1709 grand pensionary Heinsius secured his election as one of the pastors of the Walloon church at The Hague, intending to employ him mainly in civil affairs, including a secret negotiation with Marshal d'Uxelles, French plenipotentiary at the congress of Utrecht. He wrote a history of the Reformed churches and on Jewish antiquities, and is especially remembered for his debate with Bossuet.

Samuel Basnage (1638–1721) — Samuel Basnage was born at Bayeux in 1638 and died at Zutphen in 1721. A Reformed minister at Vaucelles and Bayeux, he followed his father Antoine to Holland after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685, and in April 1686 founded the Walloon church at Zutphen. He became emeritus in 1718 and opposed Jurieu's doctrines before the Synod of Haarlem in 1695. His works include Exercitationes historico-criticae de rebus sacris et ecclesiasticis (Utrecht, 1692) and Annales politico-ecclesiastici (Rotterdam, 1706). The two pages held here come from that critical-historical work: notes on ninth-century St. Gall poets.
b.s: The pieces held here are his critical apparatus printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina: notes and observations defending the authenticity of texts such as Faustus of Riez's letter to Leontius and Lucidus's letter and abjuration, taking a middle position between Sirmundus and Mauguinus on Faustus's doctrine of grace and opposing Baronius.

b.bio: The library holds one item under the name Joseph Bertinelli, a dedication letter printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 58), among the works of the Latin Fathers. The biographical surviving records under similar names do not fit this figure: they describe an eighteenth-century Italian Jesuit man of letters named Giuseppe Maria (Saverio) Bettinelli, a British Catholic priest Joseph Berington, and a Huguenot chess writer Joseph Bertin — different persons, centuries, and bodies of work, all to be disregarded here. Nothing in the sources establishes dates, offices, or a career for the author of this letter.
b.s: The single work held here is a dedication letter preserved in PL 58; its value lies in its attachment to the patristic volume it introduces rather than in any independent corpus.

w: Preface to the History of the Jerusalem Journey

b.t: Catholic scholarly editor (inferred from the work's character and its placement among Latin Fathers; not independently confirmed)
b.bio: The surviving records concern other people (La Rochepozay, Jean Bolland, Jean Beleth, Jean Bayet) and give no biographical details for Jean Besly, so no dates or offices are asserted here. What is certain from the library record is that he wrote a critical preface to a history of the First Crusade (De hierosolymitana itinere), arguing that the anonymous 'Gesta' author was Peter Tudebode, that Tudebode uniquely preserved Poitevin deeds at Antioch, that the anonymous author was the first and most trustworthy crusade historian, and that he finished before Godfrey's death in 1100.
b.s: His preface is an early piece of textual criticism on the First Crusade chronicles, weighing Albert of Aachen, Baldric, Guibert, Robert the Monk, and Raymond of Aguilers against one another and arguing against earlier authorities and editors such as Bongars, Conrad of Ursperg, Otto of Freising, Robert the Monk, and Paulus Aemilius.

b.bio: Jérôme Bignon, born in Paris on 24 August 1589 and died 7 April 1656, was a French magistrate and erudite. A precocious scholar, he published a description of the Holy Land at about age ten and was placed as companion to the dauphin, the future Louis XIII. He studied law, wrote a treatise on the precedency of the kings of France (1610), and in 1613 edited, with learned notes, the Formulae of the Merovingian jurist Marculf. He served as advocate-general to the grand council (1620), councillor of state, and advocate-general to the parlement of Paris (1626), before Richelieu appointed him to charge of the royal library in 1642.
b.s: The works under his name in this library are his 1613 annotated edition of Marculf's Formulae: the 'Bignon Formulas' reproduce the Merovingian legal forms (manumission, wergild, betrothal per Salic law) and the Preface is his editorial introduction, so he matters here as the learned editor who made these Frankish legal documents accessible.

b.bio: Justus Henning Böhmer was born in Hanover on 29 January 1674 and studied law at the University of Jena from 1693. He lectured briefly at Rinteln before moving to Halle, where he completed his licenciate in civil and church law on 27 August 1699 under teachers including Christian Thomasius. He became associate professor at Halle on 27 July 1701 and died there on 23 August 1749 as chancellor of the Duchy of Magdeburg and head of the law faculty. A jurist working chiefly on Roman and canon law, he was the first to show how older canonical principles could be adapted to post-Reformation Protestant church law. The two short pieces held here are his prefatory matter to an edition of medieval canonical collections: they survey the transmission of the ancient code of canons, compare Cresconius's nomocanon with the Mainz code, describe Burchard of Worms's arrangement of canons by subject rather than chronology, Ivo of Chartres's expansion against Berengar's heresy, Gratian's dialectical harmonizing of conflicting canons, and the papal corrections of the Decretum.
b.s: The works here are editorial prolegomena to the medieval canonists (Burchard, Ivo, Gratian) that explain how each collection ordered and corrected its sources — useful orientation for anyone reading the Decretum of Ivo in this volume.

w: Dissertation on the Book on the Body and Blood of the Lord

b.bio: Jacques Boileau was born in Paris on 16 March 1635, brother of the poet Nicolas Boileau. He studied at the Collège d'Harcourt, entered the Sorbonne's theology faculty, served as its prior from March 1660 to March 1661, and took his doctorate in May 1662. For about twenty-five years he was dean, grand vicar, and official of the diocese of Sens, receiving a canonry at the Sainte-Chapelle in 1694. He wrote on church discipline, often under pseudonyms such as Marcellus Ancyranus and Claudius Fontejus.
b.s: His dissertation here defends Ratramnus's authorship of the ninth-century treatise De corpore et sanguine Domini, arguing from inscribed manuscript evidence that the work is not John Scotus Eriugena's and that no heresy context motivated a false attribution.

b.bio: Jean Bolland (Johannes Bollandus), born at Julémont near Liège, entered the Jesuits at Mechelen in 1612, studied theology at Leuven, and was ordained by 1625. In 1630 he was sent to Antwerp to take up the hagiographical project of Héribert Rosweyde; the first volume of the Acta Sanctorum appeared there in 1643. He compiled the January volumes himself before calling Henschen and Papebroch to assist, founding what became the Bollandists. Britannica gives his birth date as 18 August 1596 at Tirlemont; Wikipedia and Schaff give 13 August at Julémont — a disagreement over day and place, not year.
b.s: The works held here are his critical prolegomena and notices prefacing patristic texts in Migne — chiefly on Caesarius of Arles, whose Life he attributes to Cyprian of Toulon with Firminus and Viventius (and the second book to Messianus and Stephanus), arguing against Baronius, Noris, and others.

b.bio: Jacques Bongars was born at Orléans in 1554 and brought up in the Reformed faith. He studied at Marburg and Jena, and after returning to France continued at Orléans and Bourges. He spent time in Rome and traveled in eastern Europe. From 1586/1587 he served Henry of Navarre (later Henry IV) as a diplomat, sent on missions to obtain men and money from the German princes and from Elizabeth I of England; from 1593 to 1610 he acted as French representative at the courts of the imperial princes, working to curtail Habsburg power. After Henry's murder in 1610 he returned to France and died at Paris on 29 July 1612. As a scholar he published an emended Justinus and compiled a history of the Crusades.
b.s: The notice held here defends William of Tyre's chronicle against critics — Heraclius of Caesarea, John Herold, and Paulus Aemilius — and belongs to Bongars' editorial work on the sources of the First Crusade and the Latin kingdom of Jerusalem.

b.bio: Jacques Bouillart was born in the Diocese of Chartres in 1669 and professed as a Benedictine monk at the Monastery of St. Faron de Meaux in 1687, later belonging to the Congregation of St.-Maur. He died on 11 December 1726. He wrote a history of the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (Paris, 1724), with biographies of its abbots from its foundation by Childeric I in 543, and edited the martyrology of Usuard, defending the genuineness of the Saint-Germain manuscript against the Jesuit hagiographer Jean Baptiste du Sollier.
b.s: The work held here is the Prolegomena to his edition of Usuard's martyrology, in which he argued for the authenticity of the Saint-Germain-des-Prés manuscript against Du Sollier.

b.bio: Jean-Jacques Bourassé, abbé, born at Sainte-Maure (Indre-et-Loire) on 22 December 1813 and died at Tours on 4 October 1872, was a French priest, archaeologist and historian. Ordained in 1838, he taught natural sciences at the preparatory seminary of Tours from 1835 and became a pioneer of Christian archaeology in France; he was a canon of Tours and of Nevers, founder and president of the Société archéologique de Touraine, and a corresponding member of the Comité des travaux historiques et scientifiques. His published works include Archéologie Chrétienne (1841) and Les Cathédrales de France (1843), and with Pierre-Désiré Janvier he issued an illustrated French translation of the Vulgate Bible (1843). The two prefaces held here are his editorial apparatus for the Migne Patrologia Latina volume of Hildebert of Lavardin's works.
b.s: The works here are not theological treatises but Bourassé's prefatory scholarship for PL 171: historical and polemical prolegomena defending Hildebert of Tours against misattributions and doctrinal slanders.

b.bio: Johann Alexander Brassicanus (family name Köl or Köll, Latinized Brassicanus) was a German Catholic humanist and Neo-Latin poet, probably born at Cannstatt around 1500 into an old Konstanz family. Educated by his father, the grammarian Johannes Brassicanus, he matriculated at Tübingen on 13 January 1514, took his M.A. in 1517, and was crowned poet laureate by Emperor Maximilian in 1518. He taught rhetoric at Vienna from about 1518, later took a doctorate in law, and served as dean of the juridical faculty (1533/34 and 1537). He edited writings of the early Fathers and died at Vienna on 25 November 1539.
b.s: The single epistle held here shows him as a patristic editor: it praises the first editor despite textual faults and offers allegorical exegesis (waters as baptism, angels anagogically), surveying citations from Eucherius, Theodoret, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola and others.

b.bio: Michel Jean Joseph Brial, called Dom Brial, was born at Perpignan on 26 May 1743 and died in Paris on 24 May 1828. He entered the Benedictines of the Congregation of Saint-Maur at the Daurade in Toulouse in 1764, was ordained priest at Bazas in 1770, and moved to Paris in October 1771 to work on the continuation of the Recueil des historiens des Gaules et de la France begun by Martin Bouquet, editing volumes 14 to 18. He also continued the Histoire littéraire de la France.
b.s: He is not a Latin Father but the nineteenth-century editor whose manuscript notices accompany Migne's Patrologia Latina; the single page held here is such a notice for PL 211, identifying and describing the manuscripts behind the printed texts.

b.bio: John Capgrave (21 April 1393 – 12 August 1464) was an English Augustinian friar, historian and theologian, born at Bishop's Lynn in Norfolk. He professed at Lynn around 1410 and was ordained priest in 1417 or 1418 (one source gives 1416 or 1417). He studied theology at his order's school in London and at Cambridge, lectured in theology, became a doctor of divinity, prior of Bishop's Lynn, and provincial of his order in England; he made at least one journey to Rome described in his Solace of Pilgrims. Older literature credits him with the Nova Legenda Angliae, but since 1970 it has been known that this collection was compiled by John of Tynemouth, a Benedictine; Capgrave only edited it. His own undoubted works include an English Life of St Katharine.
b.s: The two items shelved here under his name — a life of St Aldhelm (PL 89) and an appendix of miracles (PL 155) defending the catholic Easter date against British error and clearing Pope Sergius of slander by an infant's miraculous speech — are Aldhelm material printed in Migne, not works of the Lynn friar; readers should attribute them to Aldhelm.

b.bio: None of The surviving records describes a Giovanni Battista Carusi matching this record: they cover a modern archaeologist named Giovanni Caruso (born 1969), the Franciscan Giovanni Battista Chiodini (died 1652), the humanist Giovanni Battista Cantalicio (c. 1450–1515), and the archaeologist Giovanni Battista de Rossi (1822–1894). The library's single held work is a historical-critical note on Geoffrey Malaterra and his history of the Normans in Sicily, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 149, arguing against Vossius and citing Ordericus Vitalis, Baronius, Pirrus, Surita, and Pistorius. It belongs to early modern antiquarian scholarship on Norman Italian chronicles.
b.s: His note on Malaterra situates that chronicle of the Norman conquest of Sicily within seventeenth-century debates over its date, authorship, and reliability.

b.bio: Born and died at Liège, Jean Chapeauville studied philosophy at Cologne and Louvain, taking the Licentiate of Theology at the latter. Ordained a priest, he served as synodal examiner (1578) and parish priest of St. Michael's, Liège, became a canon of St. Peter's (1582), its provost (1599), first penitentiary canon of St. Lambert's Cathedral by appointment of Sixtus V (1587), and archdeacon of Famenne (1600). Nominated Inquisitor of the Faith in 1582, he was made vicar general by Bishop Ernest of Bavaria in 1598 and retained in that office under Ferdinand of Bavaria. He taught theology in monasteries of the diocese and worked to enforce the Tridentine reforms.
b.s: The library holds only a historical notice printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 149); Chapeauville matters chiefly as a Liège diocesan historian and reforming administrator rather than as a patristic author.

w: Index to St. Bruno's Commentary on the Psalms

b.bio: Born Johann Dobneck at Wendelstein near Nuremberg, he took the surname Cochlaeus from his birthplace. Educated at Cologne from 1504, he was rector of St. Lawrence's Latin school in Nuremberg, where he published school manuals including the Tetrachordum Musices. He took a doctorate at Ferrara (1517), was ordained priest at Rome, became dean at Frankfurt in 1520, later canon at Mainz and court chaplain to Duke George of Saxony. From 1520 until his death at Breslau he was one of Luther's leading Catholic opponents. Note on the shelf: the index to Bruno's psalms commentary printed in PL 142 sits far outside his lifetime; it is almost certainly editorial apparatus bound into the volume rather than his own composition.
b.s: He matters as the foremost early Catholic controversialist against Luther, though the single item held here is a seven-page index to St. Bruno's Commentary on the Psalms in PL 142, not one of his polemics.

w: Notes on the Book on the Deaths of the Persecutors

b.bio: Johan(nes) Columbus was born in 1640 and died in 1684. One bookseller's account describes him as a Swedish-born professor of Latin poetry working in Germany. The sources consulted say little else about him, and none describes the Lactantius material held here, so the attribution of these works to this man rests on name and period alone. The library's two works under this name are philological and historical notes on Lactantius printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 7: annotations on the De Mortibus Persecutorum (23 pp.) and shorter notes on Lactantius generally (2 pp.).
b.s: The works here are scholarly annotations on Lactantius, engaging Baluze's edition and arguing points such as the authenticity of De Mortibus Persecutorum and that Lactantius's name was Caecilius, not Caelius.

b.bio: The library prints this name as Joannes Egones and holds three volumes under it (PL 139, PL 142, PL 143), all described in the record only as 'Historical notice'. A tentative identification of this printed name with Johannes Hymonides, called John the Deacon of Rome, is plausible but not verified by any surviving records. If that identification is correct, he was probably Roman and from a wealthy family, owning an estate with an oratory in the Suburra; a learned figure at the papal Curia in the second half of the ninth century, closely associated with Anastasius Bibliothecarius, briefly exiled after the death of Nicholas I at the instance of Emperor Louis II and recalled by Adrian II; and at the request of Pope John VIII he wrote a four-book life of Gregory the Great, drawing on Gregory's own writings and on extracts from his letters preserved in the Roman archives. The other authors named in the sources (Molanus, Busaeus, Teutonicus) are different men and are disregarded here.
b.s: If identified with Johannes Hymonides, his Vita Gregorii, written at Pope John VIII's request and divided into life, pontificate, teaching, and progress in perfection, is a principal early medieval biography of Gregory the Great. Note, however, that the library record lists no copy of the Vita Gregorii under this name.

b.bio: Johann August Ernesti, born at Tennstädt in Thuringia in 1707 and died at Leipzig in 1781, was a Lutheran theologian and philologist. Educated at Schulpforta, Wittenberg, and Leipzig, he taught at the Thomasschule before holding chairs of ancient literature (1742), rhetoric (1756), and finally theology (1759) at Leipzig. He is remembered chiefly for insisting on strict philological interpretation of Scripture, especially the New Testament, separating Old Testament from New Testament hermeneutics. The work held here is not one of his biblical treatises but a preface he wrote for an edition of patristic texts, surveying how humanist scholars from Erasmus to Melanchthon joined classical and patristic study.
b.s: The preface here documents Ernesti's account of how the revival of letters restored patristic study and purity of doctrine, tracing a line from Erasmus through Mosellanus, Borner, Camerarius, and Melanchthon to Luther's dispute with Eck.

w: Bibliographical notice on the works of Rabanus

b.bio: Johann Albert Fabricius was born in Leipzig on 11 November 1668, son of Werner Fabricius, director of music at St. Paul's church there. Educated at Quedlinburg and the University of Leipzig (master of philosophy, 1689), he first made his name with the Decas decadum (1689), a survey of plagiarists and pseudonymous writers. He went to Hamburg in 1693 and served as librarian to J. F. Mayer from 1694, then taught ethics and rhetoric at the city gymnasium from 1699 until his death on 30 April 1736. In 1719 he declined a theology chair at Giessen when the Hamburg magistrates raised his salary. His Bibliothecae and related surveys made him the leading bibliographer of his century.
b.s: The works held here are Fabricius's introductory and bibliographical notices prefixed to volumes of Migne's Patrologia Latina, including his notice on Rabanus Maurus's works; a reader should treat them as informed eighteenth-century summaries of each author's life, writings, and standing.

w: On the Feast of St. Bernard

b.bio: J.G. Fatati is known here only from his own work, which identifies him as secretary of the Sacred Congregation of Rites and cites a decree of that congregation under Pope Pius VIII concerning Archbishop Opizzoni of Bologna and Prefect Pedicinius. the surviving records for this name describe instead Antonio Fatati (c. 1410–1484), bishop of Teramo, Siena, and Ancona e Numana, beatified in 1795; that fifteenth-century prelate is a different person and is not the author of the work held here.
b.s: His piece in this library is a short historical response arguing that Bernard was omitted from the litanies of the doctors, written from within the Congregation of Rites during the Pius VIII era.

b.bio: Giusto Fontanini, born at San Daniele del Friuli on 30 October 1666 and died in Rome on 11 April 1736, was an Italian Roman Catholic archbishop and historian, ordained on 23 December 1690 and consecrated titular Archbishop of Ancyra by Benedict XIII on 5 September 1725. He was a bibliophile and a defender of the Papal Curia, notably in the 1708 controversy with the Este dukes and Austria over Comacchio. He made claims about Chromatius of Aquileia (including his birthplace), about Valerian's nineteen-year tenure of the Aquileian see from A.D. 366, and about the proper conduct of episcopal condemnation. The two pieces this library files under his name are not his compositions but corrections directed against him, disputing those claims.
b.s: A reader holding these pages should read them as scholarly rejoinders to Fontanini's positions on Chromatius and Valerian of Aquileia, not as works by Fontanini himself.

b.bio: Frobenius Forster was a Bavarian Benedictine of St. Emmeram at Ratisbon: he took vows there on 8 Dec. 1728, adopting the name Frobenius, was ordained priest in 1733, then professor of philosophy and theology at his monastery, professor of philosophy and physics at Salzburg from 1745, librarian and prior from 1750, and finally Prince-Abbot. He joined the Bavarian Academy of Sciences in 1759 and wrote on philosophy and physics as well as Scripture. The works printed under his name in PL 100–101 are not patristic texts but his editorial apparatus for Alcuin: dissertations, admonitions, prefaces, an index, and a eulogy, arguing among other things that Alcuin lived past 809, was a Benedictine monk and deacon but never a priest, and that his true name was Albinus or Alchuinus.
b.s: His edition of Alcuin is the text carried in PL 100–101; these pages carry his case against D. Madrisius, Chifflet, and Walchius on Alcuin's life and authorship.

b.bio: Two men named Jean Garet are often merged under this name: a Louvain Augustinian canon who died January 21, 1571 and wrote against Protestantism, and a French Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint-Maur (1627–1694). The work held here — a two-page dedication letter printed with the Cassiodorus edition in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 69 — belongs to the second: the Maurist Garet edited Cassiodorus's complete works, and the letter cites Cassiodorus three times and Tacitus and Theodoric once each. The anti-Protestant treatises by the earlier Garet listed elsewhere under this name are not held here.
b.s: His Cassiodorus edition was still being used as the basis for Migne's 1848 collected edition of Cassiodorus, indicating its continued standing into the nineteenth century; the piece held here is its dedicatory letter.

w: Excerpts from the prefaces of the Oxford edition
Index to the letters of John of Salisbury
Second Table in the Letters of St. Thomas
Table of the Letters of Gilbert Foliot
Table of the Letters of St. Thomas

b.bio: John Allen Giles, printed here in Latinized form as Joannes Allen Gillesius, was an English historian and editor, born at Southwick House, in the parish of Mark, Somerset, and educated at Charterhouse and Corpus Christi College, Oxford, where he took a double first in 1828 and was elected fellow on 15 November 1832. Ordained to the curacy of Cossington, Somerset, after abandoning plans for the bar, he held school headships at Camberwell Collegiate School and the City of London School before devoting himself chiefly to editing medieval texts, including Bede's Ecclesiastical History and a revised translation of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. The pieces under this name in this collection are short editorial apparatus — prefaces, indices, letter-tables, and chronological catalogues — appearing in Migne's Patrologia volumes.
b.s: The works held here are not theological treatises but brief editorial apparatus for PL 190, 199, 201, 207, and 89: prefaces, letter-tables, and indices connected with the correspondence of John of Salisbury, Gilbert Foliot, and Thomas Becket materials, per the library record.

b.bio: Joannes Gremaud appears here as the author of an eleven-page historical and literary notice printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina, volume 188. The notice concerns a twelfth-century bishop of Lausanne, and its content is recoverable from the loci it treats: the foundation of Cîteaux in 1098 to restore Benedictine observance, the definitive constitution of the Cistercian order in 1119, the founding of Hautecombe in 1125 and its reform in 1135, and the episcopal career of his subject — chosen by unanimous clerical and popular acclamation, confirmed by papal precept despite reluctance, and preserving love of study within the pastoral office. It also defends the church of Lausanne's claims against royal and comital jurisdiction.
b.s: His work here is a scholarly notice establishing the biography and context of a twelfth-century bishop of Lausanne, arguing for the church's liberties against Guichenon, Manrique, and the counts of Genevois.

w: Excerpt from a Dissertation on the Council of Worms
Excerpts from the dissertation against Melchior
On the Author of the Following Short Works
Preface to the book of Paul of Bernried

b.bio: Jakob Gretser was born at Markdorf in the Diocese of Constance and entered the Society of Jesus in 1578. He spent his career at Ingolstadt, teaching philosophy for three years, dogmatic theology for fourteen, and moral theology for seven. He was regarded as one of the leading controversialists of his day, corresponded with Bellarmine and Markus Welser, and enjoyed the esteem of Clement VIII, Ferdinand II, and Maximilian I of Bavaria. Sommervogel lists 229 printed titles under his name. The works held here are his editorial apparatus for medieval texts: monuments of Saint Henry, an apology for Gregory VII, prefaces to Paul of Bernried and Bernold's short works, a life of Gerhoh, and dissertations against Henry IV's partisans.
b.s: The volumes here show Gretser as editor and polemicist for Gregorian reform material: he defends Gregory VII against Guibert and Henry IV, dates the Eberhard diplomas (early 1014 by indiction; 1019 at Bamberg), and argues for episcopal immunity from secular jurisdiction and perpetual church possession of confirmed goods — against Henry IV, Guibert, Lutherans, Calvinists, Aventinus, and Illyricus, citing Baronius and Bellarmine throughout.

b.bio: Joannes Grialius appears here as an editor of works attributed to Isidore of Seville: the pieces held under his name are prefatory matter — a dedicatory letter, admonition, and address to the reader — for a printed edition of Isidore's opuscula (PL 82). In them he defends Isidore's authorship of De ortu et obitu patrum and De conflictu vitiorum against unnamed grave men who doubted or denied it, argues that the mysticorum expositiones belong to Isidore rather than Eucherius, and answers Louvain theologians on questions of chronology and textual variants. He cites Ildephonsus, Braulio, Sigebert, Bede, Jerome, and Ambrose as witnesses.
b.s: His prefatory letters document early modern scholarly controversy over which short works could safely be attributed to Isidore of Seville.

b.bio: the surviving records describe two different men named Girolamo — the Jesuit philologist Girolamo Lagomarsini (1698–1773) and the Florentine Dominican reformer Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498) — neither of whom matches this author and neither of whom is the person meant here. The library's holdings decide who this is: a writer whose single extant work in this library is a history of the miracles of St. John Gualbert, the eleventh-century founder of Vallombrosa. On that evidence he belongs to the circle that preserved John Gualbert's cult, probably a monk of Vallombrosa or a related house, but no source here gives his dates, office, or birthplace.
b.s: His Miracles of St. John Gualbert records how the saint's sign of the cross, intercession, and exorcised water were held to expel demons, and it states explicitly why such things were written down: only credible witnessed testimony was committed to writing, lest unwritten tradition perish.

b.bio: The author printed as Jacques Horst is Jakob Horst (Horstius), a Roman Catholic theologian and licentiate of sacred theology, born in 1537 and died in 1600. He should not be confused with the later ascetical writer Jacob Merlo Horstius (d. 1644), a different man sharing the name. His Catholicæ communionis defensio answers Friedrich Hamelmann on communion under both kinds; the catalogue classifies it under 'Lord's Supper — Communion in both elements'.
b.s: His works here are short Latin polemics against sectarian critics, arguing that the holiness of the saints confirms their doctrine and that miracles confirm true doctrine by divine power, with loci on the Church, true worship, the Lord's Supper, and justification.

b.bio: Surviving records do not clearly identify this author. They record an eighteenth-century Parisian church musician named Jacques Jérôme La Perruque, a sixteenth-century council editor, and two later French Jesuits — different people sharing similar names, not this one. What can be said comes from the library record alone: a single Latin apologetic piece, the Apologetic Hecatostichon, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 153, which defends the phrasing of a writer named Bruno against fastidious critics.
b.s: The work held here is a polemic defending Bruno's plain, devout diction, arguing that humble speech befits address to God and that penitence excludes rhetorical ornament.

b.bio:
James the Deacon (unknown) — The library record decides who this is: the works held here are the Life of Saint Pelagia, printed in Migne's PL 73 under the name James the Deacon (Jacobus Diaconus). This is not the seventh-century Roman deacon of the Gregorian mission to Northumbria who accompanied Paulinus of York and is described by Bede — that man left no such writing, and all surviving records concern only him, so they cannot be used for this author. The author of the Pelagia legend is otherwise unidentified; no surviving record gives his dates, place, or office, so none are asserted.

Eustochius the Interpreter (unknown) — Eustochius the Interpreter appears here as the author named on the Latin Life of Saint Pelagia printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 73. No surviving record gives dates or offices for this Eustochius. The sources consulted describe St. Eustochium Julia (c. 368–419/420), Jerome's correspondent and Paula's daughter at Bethlehem — a different person with a similar name, whose works do not include a Life of Pelagia; they are therefore set aside and not used for this note. The Life recounts the conversion of the actress Pelagia of Antioch: her baptism, penitential withdrawal disguised as a male recluse, and death, framing her story around repentance, satisfaction for sin before the last judgment, and salvation resting in God's mercy rather than works.
b.s: His Life of Saint Pelagia recounts the conversion of the harlot Pelagia to a hidden life of penance; it treats sin, grace, baptism (which washes the sinner white as snow), satisfaction for sins before the last judgment, salvation resting in God's mercy rather than works, and the soul adorned for the heavenly spouse.

b.bio: Johann Wilhelm Jan (also printed Janus), a Lutheran theologian born 9 November 1681 in Raben, matriculated at the University of Wittenberg in 1699, took his Magister in 1701, taught at Breslau (professor of elocution and moral philosophy from 1713) and at Wittenberg (professor of history from 1714), received his licentiate and doctorate in theology at Wittenberg in 1719, and died there on 27 August 1725. His listed writings include dissertations such as Judicia Eruditorum de Origine Electorum and De Liturgiis Orientalibus. The single item held here, a brief letter to Hoffmann printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 67 among patristic texts, does not match any of those works, so it cannot be confirmed that this early eighteenth-century Lutheran academic wrote it.
b.s: The library holds only a one-page Letter to Hoffmann under this name from PL 67; its authorship is not established by the biographical sources, which document instead an early eighteenth-century Lutheran academic.

b.bio: Jeremiah was archbishop of Sens, succeeding Magnus in 818 and dying, according to the Cyclopedia entry, in 827; the same entry says he flourished in the latter half of the 8th and early part of the 9th century. Beyond this the sources record nothing of his life. The library holds letters printed under his name in Migne's PL 105, one of which treats Christian conduct as a history arguing that without salt — presumably the salt of discipline or wisdom — the Christian life is foolish.
b.s: His surviving correspondence in PL 105 is a minor witness to Carolingian episcopal writing on Christian moral formation.

b.bio: the surviving records describe Caesarius of Arles (468/470–542), bishop of Arles and foremost ecclesiastic of Merovingian Gaul; they do not describe an author named John of Arles, so no dates or career can be asserted here. What identifies this figure is the single epistle the library holds under his name (PL 72): a short piece of exegesis and definition treating true worship, moral virtue, and eternal life, which asserts that the established rule suffices without amendment and that solitary religious must abstain from drinking with visitors, since convivial drinking opens the door to temptation.
b.s: His sole work here is a brief disciplinary letter on monastic sobriety, showing how Gallic ascetic rule governed even the hospitality shown to guests.

b.bio: John was born in Scallabis (Santarém, Portugal) of Gothic parents, according to Isidore of Seville. Educated at Constantinople for many years, he returned to Visigothic Spain, where, per Isidore and the Catholic Encyclopedia, he refused to join the Arian state church under Leovigild and was exiled to Barcelona. After Leovigild's death (586) he founded the monastery of Biclaro and later became bishop of Girona, attending synods at Saragossa (592), Barcelona (599), and Egara (614). Modern historians caution that a systematic Visigothic persecution of Catholics is poorly attested in contemporary sources, including his own Chronicle.
b.s: His Chronicle, continuing Victor of Tunnuna from 567/568 to 590, is a primary source for the reign of Leovigild, the conversion of Reccared from Arianism to Catholicism, and the anti-Arian polemic of late sixth-century Spain; the pages held here assert that conversion should come by reason not coercion and that God grants victory to the catholic faithful regardless of numbers.

w: Surnames of those who entered England

b.bio: The library prints the name as John Brampton; the sources identify him as John Brompton (or Bromton), a Cistercian monk elected abbot of Jervaulx in Yorkshire in 1436. A chronicle running from Augustine of Canterbury's arrival to the death of Richard I was printed under his name in Twysden's Decem Scriptores (1652), but its attribution rests only on an inscription in a Cambridge manuscript and may mean no more than that Brompton had the manuscript copied for his abbey; Selden likewise held the chronicle did not belong to Brompton personally, who merely procured it for his monastery. Hardy showed the compilation postdates the mid-fourteenth century, since it draws on Ralph Higden, and probably reworks an earlier compilation from the Norwich diocese. The work is uncritical and full of fables.
b.s: The single item held here, 'Surnames of those who entered England' (PL 149), is not the chronicle discussed by the sources; readers should treat its ascription with caution and should not assume this author is the Jervaulx abbot or the supposed chronicler.

b.bio: John Canaparius was a German monk of the Aventine monastery of Santi Bonifacio ed Alessio in Rome and its prior. He has long been credited with writing the first Vita sancti Adalberti episcopi Pragensis in 999, two years after Adalbert's death; the work exists in three redactions and survives in some forty-three manuscripts. Johannes Fried has challenged this attribution, arguing the Vita was written down at Liège from an archetype traceable to the imperial shrine at Aachen. The library prints the Life under his name.
b.s: The Life of St. Adalbert long attributed to him is regarded as the first hagiography of the Prague bishop-missionary, contrasting true worship with pagan idolatry and nominal Christianity, and recording Adalbert's route along the Vistula to Gdańsk.

w: Rule of the Military Order of Aviz

b.bio: João (John) Cirita, a hermit of Galician origin who became a monk and abbot at São João de Tarouca in Portugal, is credited with bringing the Cistercian reform to the Iberian Far West. The sources date his activity to the later twelfth century; he corresponded with King Alphonsus, the archbishop of Braga, and the abbots of Cîteaux and Clairvaux. He is also credited with drafting the Rule for the military Order of Aviz, binding its knights to Benedictine observance under royal dominion while reserving appeals to the pope. A cultus developed around him, but firm biographical detail remains sparse.
b.s: The work held here, the Rule of the Military Order of Aviz, shows how a Cistercian abbot adapted monastic discipline for a fighting order: hope resting in faith rather than arms, spoils assigned to the poor and churches, captives won by admonition.

w: Letter to Geoffrey, Richard, and the monks of Savigny

b.bio: None of The surviving records describes the author of this letter. They concern three unrelated men who share or resemble the name: an eighteenth-century Maltese Franciscan philosopher (John Constance Parnis), a Dominican auxiliary bishop of Cologne who died in 1321, and Bernard of Constance, the eleventh-century schoolmaster of Constance and Hildesheim. The letter held here is addressed to Geoffrey, Richard, and the monks of Savigny, treats computus, and argues that ancient computational tables sometimes fail and that computus serves in confuting heretics.
b.s: The single page held under this name is a brief computistical letter to the monks of Savigny, notable for admitting errors in ancient tables and for framing calendar reckoning as a weapon against heretics.

b.bio: The library holds under this name a two-page hagiographical text from PL 155 recounting a saint's life: it cites Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and Count Eustace of Boulogne, and notes that Godfrey and Baldwin ruled crusader Jerusalem, which places its subject among the kin circle of the counts of Boulogne around the turn of the twelfth century. Surviving records do not clearly identify this author. They instead cover John Guillim, an early seventeenth-century English herald; John of Genoa, the Dominican grammarian; John Slotanus, a Dutch Dominican polemicist; and John Marchesinus, a Franciscan biblical glossator — all different men with similar names, to be ignored here.
b.s: The single short text held here is a saint's life built on themes of healing at the tomb, restoration of what sin has lost through a saint's merits, and eternal reward prepared for the blessed.

b.bio: John I was a Tuscan by birth, son of Constantius, elected bishop of Rome on 13 August 523 after an interregnum of seven days. As a deacon he had sided with the Antipope Laurentius and wrote a libellus to Pope Symmachus in 506 confessing his error in opposing him. In 525 he negotiated in standardizing the Western calculation of Easter with the help of the monk Dionysius Exiguus, ratifying the Alexandrian computation. King Theoderic sent him on a diplomatic mission to Constantinople to negotiate better treatment for Arians under Emperor Justin; on his return to Ravenna Theoderic imprisoned him, and he died there of neglect and ill-treatment.
b.s: The work held here is a letter concerning despoiled bishops and church property: it argues that the despoiled cannot be summoned or judged, that despoiled bishops must be fully restored, that property invaders must restore with multiplication, and that Arian churches may be reconsecrated as catholic — positions set against the Arians, the rivals of Symmachus, and King Theoderic.

b.bio: Born Mercurius in Rome, son of Praeiectus, he was a priest at St. Clement's Basilica before his election as bishop of Rome on 2 January 533, succeeding Boniface II after an eleven-week contest marred by bribery with church funds and the sale of sacred vessels. He was the first pope to take a new name on elevation, dropping his pagan birth name for that of a martyred John. His brief pontificate removed Bishop Contumeliosus of Riez from office, convened a council on readmitting Arian clergy, and approved Justinian's edict condemning the Acoemetae monks' Nestorian position.
b.s: His doctrinal ruling against the Acoemeti — affirming that one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh and that Mary is truly Mother of God — addressed a controversy entangled with his predecessor Hormisdas's earlier rejection of that phrase; the letters held here defend that Christology against Nestorius, the Acoemetae, and Eutyches, alongside canons penalizing simony in episcopal elections.

b.bio: John III, born Catelinus in Rome to a distinguished family (his father Anastasius was a vir illustris), was bishop of Rome from his consecration on 17 July 561 until his death on 13 July 574. His pontificate coincided with the Lombard invasion of Italy beginning in 568; he fled to Naples and later withdrew to the catacombs during the quarrel over Narses' defense of Rome. Nearly all records of his reign perished in the invasion. At King Guntram's urging he restored the bishops Salonius of Embrun and Sagittarius of Gap, who had been condemned at a synod of Lyons (c. 567). The two letters held here concern church order: they argue that only bishops as successors of the apostles confer the Holy Spirit, that the example of the seventy forbids chorepiscopal confirmation, that pontifical power passes to a single successor, and that three bishops plus the metropolitan are required for ordination.
b.s: His surviving correspondence is among the few witnesses to his pontificate and shows sixth-century Roman claims about episcopal succession and the suppression of chorepiscopi.

b.bio: John IV was a native of Iadera in Dalmatia, son of the advocate Venantius, and archdeacon of the Roman Church when elected bishop of Rome; he was consecrated on 24 December 640 and died on 12 October 642. His birth year is not securely recorded. While still pope-elect he wrote to the clergy of Ireland and Scotland correcting their reckoning of Easter. He sent Abbot Martin to Dalmatia and Istria to ransom captives taken in Slav invasions. The letters held here defend a single will in Christ's humanity against the Monothelites and the patriarchs Sergius and Pyrrhus, and assert against Pelagians that no man is without sin except Christ alone.
b.s: His letters are early Roman responses to Monothelitism, insisting on one will in Christ's humanity rather than two contrary wills.

w: Canon on the election of the Pope
Opening Address at the Council of Ravenna

b.bio: John IX was born around 825; his birthplace is disputed (Wikipedia says Tivoli, Britannica says Rome), and he was son of a man named Rampoald(o). A Benedictine priest ordained by Pope Formosus, he was elected pope in early 898 with the backing of the ducal house of Spoleto, over the rival candidate Sergius (later Sergius III), whom he excommunicated. His brief pontificate undid the Cadaver Synod of Stephen VI: councils at Rome and Ravenna in 898 burned that synod's acts, restored clergy degraded by Stephen, forbade re-ordinations, and confirmed the Constitutio Romana requiring an imperial emissary at papal consecrations.
b.s: The works here are letters and conciliar texts from his short pontificate, chiefly against Photius and his ordinations, asserting papal authority over all churches and the binding force of successive popes' decrees.

b.bio: None of The surviving records identifies this author; they describe other men called 'of Marsica' — the humanist Giovanni Armonio Marso (c. 1477–c. 1553), the historian Muzio Febonio (1597–1663), and Cardinal Leo of Ostia (1046–1115/7) — none of whom matches these works. The library record itself fixes who this is: an adherent of Pope Gregory VII's party in the Investiture Controversy, writing against Henry IV of Germany when the pontiff was held captive by his enemies.
b.s: His two pieces here are short polemical exhortations of the Gregorian cause: a letter to Richard of Albano and an address to the Roman people defending the apostolic see and justifying armed resistance to Henry.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies an author called 'John of Michaelis'. The sources describe unrelated men: Johann David Michaelis (1717–1791), Göttingen professor of Oriental languages; his father Johann Heinrich Michaelis (1668–1738), Halle Hebraist; and John of Hildesheim (d. 1375), Carmelite author of the Historia Trium Regum. None wrote on the Templars, so none is this author. What can be said rests on the library record alone: under this name it holds eight pages from PL 166 containing the Latin Rule of the Templars.
b.s: The held text is the early Latin Rule of the Knights Templar, which records the council's approval of the order's rule, prescribes Lord's Prayers in place of missed office and suffrages for dead brothers, forbids other death-offerings to templars, and grounds the order's origin in Christ.

w: History of the Translation of St. Glodesind of Metz
Life of Saint Glodesind of Metz

b.bio: John succeeded Anste as abbot of Saint-Arnoul at Metz in 960 and died about 977; Deutsche Biographie gives his death only as before 984. He was reputed learned and liberal for his time, granting a charter of freedom to the serfs of Maurville. The works held here identify him as the hagiographer: his Life of John of Gorze records the abbot who reformed Gorze from 933 and served as Otto I's envoy to Córdoba, and his two pieces on Glodesind treat the Metz saint's life and the translation of her relics.
b.s: His Vita of John of Gorze is a principal source for the tenth-century Gorze monastic reform and for contacts between Ottonian Germany and Muslim Spain.

w: Vision of the State of Souls

b.bio: No surviving record identifies a 'John of Saint-Laurent of Liège.' The sources describe two different monks of Saint-Laurent Abbey in Liège: Renier of Saint-Laurent (died 1188), a writer of theological, exegetical, historical, and hagiographical works, and Jean de Stavelot (Johannes de Stabulis, 1388–1449), a monk, chronicler, copyist, and illuminator. Neither source attributes to either man the Vision of the State of Souls held here. The library record alone shows that this author's single held work treats last things: postmortem fates by merit, purgatorial penance with relief after torment, demons dwelling in aerial places, and the sign of the cross against demonic illusion.
b.s: The Vision of the State of Souls is an otherworld vision arguing for graded postmortem fates and purgatorial relief, citing Maurice, Bede, and Paul.

b.bio: John of Sabina was Bishop of Sabina whom a Roman faction elected as pope in opposition to Benedict IX in 1045, reportedly after payment of money. Benedict drove him from Rome with troops; he returned to his see and continued pressing claims during the pontificate of Gregory VI. At the synod of Sutri in 1046, convened by Emperor Henry III, he was deprived of all sacerdotal rank and confined to a monastery for life. The work held here is his complaint against the abbot of Farfa over jurisdiction and rights in a shared church.
b.s: His complaint against the Farfenses is a concrete record of episcopal-versus-monastic jurisdiction disputes in eleventh-century Latium, asserting that a diocesan bishop holds jurisdiction over churches in his see.

w: Letter to Vladimir, King of the Rus

b.bio: Joannes Smera Polovecius is known to Migne's Patrologia Latina only through a brief notice on his life and works (PL 151, cols. 1405–1406B) and a single letter, printed in PL 151 (cols. 1405–1410A), both dated to around 990. The sources give no birthplace, office, or dates beyond this approximate year. The letter is addressed to Wladimir, king of the Rus, and argues in Latin against the Greeks and their patriarchs.
b.s: The library holds his Letter to Vladimir, King of the Rus — a Latin polemic urging the Rus toward the Latin church, asserting that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, that the true church is the new Israel of God, that Christ is Son of God and judge, that Slavs will embrace the Christian faith while Greek 'idolaters' perish eternally, and that converted Jews will obtain salvation.

b.bio: Born Johann Heidenberg at Trittenheim on the Moselle, he entered the Benedictines at Sponheim at about twenty and was elected abbot the following year. He built Sponheim's library into one of the most renowned in Europe while pressing monastic reform that provoked lasting opposition in his community; in 1503 he resigned and moved to St. Jacob zu den Schotten at Würzburg, where he was elected abbot in 1506. He wrote more than eighty works — chronicles, catalogues of ecclesiastical writers, and cryptographic treatises — and counted Celtis, Reuchlin, and von Dalberg among his friends.
b.s: The works held here are his hagiographical and bibliographical labors: the first continuous life of Rabanus Maurus, lives of Rupert, Haymo, and Smaragdus, and entries for his catalogue of church writers, through which much Carolingian monastic memory survives.

w: Letter to the bishops of Britain

b.bio: An ethnic Greek from Rossano in Calabria, son of Plato, curator of the Palatine Hill for the Byzantine emperor, and of Blatta. Before his elevation he was rector of the papal patrimony on the Appian Way. He was bishop of Rome from 1 March 705 until his death on 18 October 707, restored and adorned Sancta Maria Antiqua and other Roman churches, and did not recognize the canons of the Quinisext Council of 692 submitted by Justinian II. A caution on attribution: the two letters held here name Archbishop Theodore of Canterbury and cite Agatho, Wilfrid, Hilda, and Berthwald — figures whose affairs belong to the 690s, before this pontificate; the correspondence with the English church over Wilfrid is more commonly assigned to his predecessor John VI.
b.s: The letters here assert Roman primacy in episcopal disputes — that appeal to the apostolic see settles them and contempt of conciliar summons brings deposition — addressed to the Anglo-Saxon church.

b.bio: The library prints the name as John of Venice; the author is the deacon Johannes who wrote around 1008 and was close to Doge Pietro Orseolo II (991–1008). His chronicle is the first work of Venetian historiography, though its earliest manuscripts name neither title nor author; it has been printed as Chronicon Venetum et Gradense and Istoria Veneticorum, and in older literature as il Sagornino after a 1765 edition's misattribution. He is not the Roman deacon John Hymonides (d. before 882), biographer of Gregory the Great, nor any of the other Italian Johns called 'the Deacon'.
b.s: His Chronicle of Venice and Grado is the earliest Venetian history and the source later chroniclers drew on for the city's origins: the flight from the Lombard invasions to the islands, the translation of the patriarchal see from Aquileia to Grado, and Grado's metropolitan rank by synod and papal consent.

b.bio: John X was born at Tossignano in Romagna, served as Archbishop of Ravenna from about 905, and became pope in March 914 as a candidate of the Tusculan nobility. He organized the alliance that defeated the Saracens at the Garigliano and fell out with Marozia, who had him deposed, imprisoned, and murdered; he died in Rome on 28 May 928. One source gives his death as 2 July 929. The letters held here concern episcopal elections, monastic exemption, and the defense of church property against secular seizure.
b.s: The privileges printed here show an early tenth-century pope asserting canonical election by clergy and people, free abbatial election belonging to the monks themselves, and papal protection of ecclesiastical property under anathema.

b.bio: John XI became pope in March 931 through the influence of his mother Marozia, who then ruled Rome. His parentage is disputed: most sources make him Marozia's son by Duke Alberic I of Spoleto, while Liutprand of Cremona and the Liber Pontificalis call him the natural son of Pope Sergius III. After Alberic II overthrew Marozia in 932, John was confined to the Lateran and exercised only spiritual functions until his death in December 935 or January 936 (the Catholic Encyclopedia gives 936). The letters held here are papal privileges for monasteries, notably Cluny, issued under his name.
b.s: The four pages held here are privilege charters asserting direct subjection of monasteries to the Roman see, exemption from episcopal and secular lordship, free abbatial election, and anathema against violators — documents central to the tenth-century Cluniac exemption movement.

b.bio: John XII, born Octavian into the Tusculan family, was elected pope on 16 December 955 at about eighteen, the son of Alberic II, who had ruled Rome and arranged the succession. He crowned Otto I emperor in 962; after quarrelling with Otto he was deposed by a Roman synod convened by Otto in 963 in favor of Leo VIII, but died on 14 May 964 before the schism was resolved. The letters and privileges held here are administrative documents: grants to monasteries (Subiaco among them), rulings against bishops claiming jurisdiction over monastic houses, and correspondence touching Greeks and named opponents such as Isuardus.
b.s: The works held are papal privileges and letters showing tenth-century Rome's exercise of jurisdiction over monasteries and its dealings with Greek churches, not doctrinal treatises.

b.bio: John XIII, born in Rome around 930, was bishop of Narni when Emperor Otto I raised him to the papacy on 1 October 965. Roman nobles hostile to Otto kidnapped him in December 965; Otto restored him in 966 and punished his opponents. John crowned Otto II co-emperor at Christmas 967 and crowned Theophano empress immediately before her marriage to Otto II in 972. His pontificate, aligned with the imperial house, saw the emperor restore considerable territory to the Papal See. He died in Rome on 6 September 972.
b.s: The letters and decrees held here show a tenth-century pope asserting papal founding of metropolitan sees by Peter's authority, exempting clergy from secular exactions, and canonically deposing a bishop guilty of heresy and rebellion — the jurisdictional claims of the Ottonian papacy in documentary form.

b.bio: John XIV was born Peter Canepanova (or Campanora) in Pavia and served as Bishop of Pavia from 971 until Emperor Otto II named him pope in November or December 983, after Maiolus of Cluny refused the office. The appointment was made without consultation with the clergy and people of Rome and without formal election. When Otto died on 7 December 983, John lost his protector: Antipope Boniface VII returned to Rome in April 984, imprisoned him in Castel Sant'Angelo, and he died there on 20 August 984, by starvation or poisoning. His sole extant document is the letter to Archbishop Alo of Benevento held here.
b.s: The letter to Alo of Benevento is his only surviving document, setting out episcopal duties: shepherds answer for negligent oversight, justice must be impartial between rich and poor, discipline tempered by paternal love avoids cruelty, and outward honor requires inward observance.

b.bio: John XIX, born Romanus of the Counts of Tusculum in Rome, was a layman when elected pope between 12 April and 10 May 1024 on the death of his brother Benedict VIII; he received all orders in succession and was consecrated bishop that June. He crowned Conrad II emperor at Easter 1027 and supported him. His pontificate is remembered for the affair over Byzantine requests to recognize the patriarch of Constantinople as oecumenical patriarch: according to a contemporary account of questionable reliability he consented to be paid for this recognition, but public outcry forced withdrawal of the agreement. The works held here are not treatises but papal letters and diplomas: grants confirming bishoprics and property (notably to Benedict, bishop of Porto), privileges with anathema against violators, and rulings in disputes with Poppo, patriarch of Aquileia, the rival patriarch of Grado, Odilo of Cluny, Gauslenus of Mâcon, and imperial officials.
b.s: The library holds his curial correspondence and privilege-grants, primary documents of Tusculan-era papal government rather than theological writing.

b.bio: John XV, a Roman and son of the presbyter Leo, was elected pope between 6 August and 5 September 985 after the death of the usurper Boniface VII, having previously been cardinal-priest of St. Vitalis. His pontificate was overshadowed by the patrician Crescentius II, who controlled Rome; according to some chroniclers the pope fled to Tuscany to seek help from Empress Theophano before returning under Crescentius' promises. He maintained friendly relations with the Saxon emperors, protected the Cluniac monks, carried out the first solemn canonization by papal decree, and died in Rome in March or April 996. Some chroniclers invented an earlier John XV (son of Robert), which disordered the numeration of popes named John.
b.s: The letters held here are privileges for monasteries — asserting free abbatial election, exemption from episcopal jurisdiction, royal protection and immunity, and anathema against violators — documents central to the history of monastic immunity and the growth of papal authority.

b.bio: John XVIII (Giovanni Fasano or Phasianus), son of a Roman priest named Leo, was consecrated pope at Christmas 1003 and died in June or July 1009. He owed his elevation to the Roman patrician John Crescentius III, under whose influence he governed during the contest between Emperor Henry II and Arduin of Ivrea. His recorded acts are administrative: confirming possessions and privileges of churches and monasteries, consenting at the Roman Synod of June 1007 to the establishment of the See of Bamberg founded and endowed by Henry II, conferring ecclesiastical privileges on the re-established See of Merseburg, and conferring pallia on Meingaudus of Trier and Elphege of Canterbury. He abdicated for reasons not recorded and died shortly after at St. Paul Outside the Walls. The letters held here are such confirmations and privileges.
b.s: The single work held is a set of papal letters and diplomas asserting apostolic authority over monastic property: anathema on violators, exemption from secular dominion, and perpetual confirmation of imperial endowments — documents of early eleventh-century papal privilege-granting rather than doctrinal treatise.

b.bio: John of Belmeis (Jean aux Belles-Mains), a native of Canterbury, was a clerk to Theobald of Canterbury and treasurer of York from 1152. Made Bishop of Poitiers at Henry II's wish, he supported Thomas Becket in the quarrel with the king. He was elected Archbishop of Lyon in 1181, where he banned Waldensian preaching, resigned the see around 1193, and died as a Cistercian monk at Clairvaux.
b.s: The letters held here concern jurisdictional disputes with Richard, duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitou, defending the see of Lyon's full temporal jurisdiction and papal delegation of criminal (blood) jurisdiction to a steward; they also assert that executioners of blood are barred from holy orders.

w: Excerpts from the Penitential of John of God

b.bio: Johannes de Deo (John of Deo / João de Deus), called Hispanus, was born in Silves, Portugal, around 1190 and died in Lisbon on 15 March 1267. He studied canon law at Bologna under the archpriest Zoen from 1223 to 1229, then taught there for over twenty years, styling himself doctor decretorum. He held a canonry in Lisbon cathedral from 1241, served as a judge delegate for Popes Innocent IV and Alexander IV, and by March 1260 had become archdeacon of Santarém. His works include the Liber poenitentiarius de cautela simplicium sacerdotum (1247) and the widely circulated Concordantia decretorum et titulorum decretalium, completed in 1248.
b.s: The work held here is his Penitential (Liber poenitentiarius, excerpts in PL 99), a practical manual warning simple priests about the dangers of hearing confession: it holds confession valid only to one's own prelate or a licensed priest, treats contrition plus confession as obtaining remission of guilt before absolution of penalty, allows commuted penance for the sick with deferred fulfillment, and grades penances for coerced sin, slaves, and freemen, arguing against overreaching archdeacons and those who deny that popes can sin.

b.bio: John Hymonides, called John the Deacon of Rome, was probably a monk of Monte Cassino before becoming a deacon of the Roman Church and a figure at the papal Curia under Pope John VIII (872–882). He was closely associated with Anastasius Bibliothecarius. At John VIII's instance he wrote a four-book Vita Gregorii Magni, drawing on Gregory's register and on earlier extracts from Gregory's letters in the Roman archives; he also versified the apocryphal Coena Cypriani and began a lost Vita S. Clementis for Gaudericus of Velletri. A planned church history, for which Anastasius compiled Greek extracts, was never written. The library holds his account of the Lateran church, which asserts its principate over all churches and recounts Constantine's conversion through Sylvester's baptism.
b.s: His Vita Gregorii preserved extensive extracts from Gregory's register, important for the study of papal registers; the work held here is an early witness to the Lateran's claimed primacy over all churches and to the Sylvester-Constantine legend.

b.bio: John of Lodi, born at Lodi Vecchio in 1025, became a hermit in the 1060s at the Camaldolese monastery of Fonte Avellana, where he was disciple and personal secretary to Peter Damian. After Damian's death in 1072 he wrote his biography, dated 1076–1082. He served twice as prior of Fonte Avellana (1082–1084 and 1100–1101) and became Bishop of Gubbio in 1104, holding the see until his death there in 1106.
b.s: His Life of Peter Damian is the earliest biography of Damian (Vatican News describes John as Damian's first biographer) and a principal source for the reformer's childhood, monastic career, and conflicts with Milanese objectors, secularized canons, and the archbishop of Ravenna; the library copy's mined content confirms these polemical targets.

b.bio: the surviving records here describe two different twelfth-century saints named 'John the Hermit' — Juan de Ortega of Burgos (d. 1163) and John of Tufara (d. 1170) — neither of whom wrote these works. The library's record instead shows a John the Hermit to whom two hagiographical lives of Bernard of Clairvaux are attributed, both printed in PL 185. Nothing else about his dates, career, or monastic affiliation is established by the material at hand.
b.s: His works here are hagiographical lives of Bernard of Clairvaux, arguing that miracles attest the saints' merits, that saints merit honor in the church, and that their examples nourish and instruct the soul.

b.bio: The library holds one short epistle by 'John the Monk' addressed to Adalberon, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 166. The encyclopedic surviving records describe a different man of the same name: Johannes Monachus (John of Cressy), a thirteenth-century French Cistercian canonist and cardinal who died in 1313 and glossed the Sextus decretalium of Boniface VIII. That canonist cannot be identified with the author of this liturgical-allegorical epistle, so his biography is set aside as a homonym; nothing further is known here about our author.
b.s: The epistle held here reads the whole mass office as signifying Christ's nativity, distinguishing eternal from temporal nativity, asserting that the Son is coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, begotten from the Father's substance, and defending the Son's incomprehensible eternal generation against those who would dissolve the question by a three-times allegory, citing Ambrose and Amalarius.

b.bio: Jonas of Bobbio, also called Jonas of Susa, was born at Sigusia (Susa) in Piedmont around the close of the sixth century. He entered Bobbio in 618 and was soon appointed to a position of confidence, probably that of secretary to the abbots Attala (d. 627) and Bertulf, accompanying the latter to Rome in 628 to secure the abbey's exemption from episcopal jurisdiction. He then settled permanently in Gaul, assisted Amandus's mission among the heathen in what is now Belgium and northern France, wrote his Life of Columbanus between 640 and 643, and by 659 was abbot of a monastery that cannot now be determined.
b.s: His Life of Columbanus is one of the most influential works of early medieval hagiography, and his collected saints' lives — Columbanus, Eustasius, Attala, Bertulf, Burgundofara, John of Réomé — are a principal record of the Columbanian monastic movement; the works held here argue that saints' lives are written for imitation by posterity.
