b.bio: Jonas of Bobbio (c. 600 – after 659) — Jonas of Bobbio, also called Jonas of Susa, was born at Sigusia (Susa) in Piedmont around the close of the sixth century. He entered Bobbio in 618 and was soon appointed to a position of confidence, probably that of secretary to the abbots Attala (d. 627) and Bertulf, accompanying the latter to Rome in 628 to secure the abbey's exemption from episcopal jurisdiction. He then settled permanently in Gaul, assisted Amandus's mission among the heathen in what is now Belgium and northern France, wrote his Life of Columbanus between 640 and 643, and by 659 was abbot of a monastery that cannot now be determined.
b.s: His Life of Columbanus is one of the most influential works of early medieval hagiography, and his collected saints' lives — Columbanus, Eustasius, Attala, Bertulf, Burgundofara, John of Réomé — are a principal record of the Columbanian monastic movement; the works held here argue that saints' lives are written for imitation by posterity.

w: On the Origin and Deeds of the Goths

b.bio: Jordan of Limoges (Jordan of Laron) was a castellan's son from the Laron clan of Noblac, lay provost of Saint-Leonard of Noblat, elected bishop of Limoges in late January 1024 in a disputed election backed by Duke William V of Aquitaine and consecrated by the Archbishop of Bordeaux rather than his legitimate metropolitan at Bourges. He held the see until his death, dated 1051 by one source and 1052 by another. The works printed under his name in PL 142 are not securely his: Adhemar of Chabannes composed a fictional account of the 1031 Peace-council debates and published it as conciliar minutes under Jordan's name, a forgery that misled modern scholars and led to its assignment to him in the Patrologia Latina.
b.s: The Gothic history held here (PL 69) is the work of the sixth-century writer Jordanes, not this bishop; the eleventh-century Jordan's own attributions rest on Adhemar of Chabannes' forgery, so nothing here can be treated as his genuine authorship.

b.bio: Surviving records do not clearly identify this author; they cover two other twelfth-century men named Jocelin — Jocelin de Brakelond, a Benedictine chronicler of Bury St Edmunds, and Jocelin of Furness, a Cistercian hagiographer — and are therefore not used for this note. The library's own record shows a Jocelin of Tours engaged in disputes over monastic discipline and jurisdiction around the church of Tours: he defends an abbot of Bourgueil against accusers, resists the canons of St Martin who sought to stop services during a chapter judgment, and rules on appeals to the king, regalia, and abbatial elections.
b.s: His letters are evidence for how episcopal and royal authority over monks was argued in practice at Tours, citing local canons, a privilege of Louis and his father, and Benedict.

b.bio: Josephus Scottus ('the Irishman'), a monk, poet, and diplomat of the Carolingian Renaissance, was educated under Colgu at Clonmacnoise and under Alcuin at York before following Alcuin to the court of Charlemagne. In 787/8 Charlemagne sent him as an envoy (missus) to Rome, Spoleto, and Benevento, where his party narrowly escaped an ambush by Lombard agents. During Alcuin's absence in England (790–93) he sent news of Carolingian affairs and handled some business for him. He eventually became abbot of an unidentified monastery (suggested as in Switzerland or Bavaria); the Annals of Ulster obit for 794, if it is indeed his, names him 'abbot of Clúana maccu Nóis' (Clonmacnoise). Sources give differing death dates: between 791 and 804, or c. 794.
b.s: The library holds two brief verse pieces from PL 99, one citing Jerome; he is valued chiefly as Alcuin's pupil and correspondent and as a rare Irish voice at the Frankish court.

w: On the Translation of the Bodies of SS. Ragnobert and Zeno

b.bio: Josephus sacerdos ('Joseph the priest') is known only from a single short work dated 846 in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 106): an account of the translation of the bodies of Saints Ragnobert and Zeno. The text names Freculf, bishop of Lisieux, and Baltfrid as bishops involved and addresses opponents including one Herveus and a mocking priest named Gulfuidus. Note: sources describing 'Joseph Scottus', an Irish deacon at Charlemagne's court who died between 791 and 804, concern a different person with a similar name and were not used for this note.
b.s: His sole surviving work is a Carolingian relic-translation narrative defending the move by appeal to divine visions, scriptural curse on scoffers, incorrupt vestments, and miracles worked at the saints' bodies.

w: Lament on the Passing of Odilo

b.bio: Jotsald (Iotsaldus) was a Benedictine monk of Cluny in the eleventh century, the first biographer of Abbot Odilo of Cluny. He wrote a Life of Odilo and a short lament on the abbot's death, both preserved in Migne's Patrologia Latina (vol. 142). The Life presents Odilo's sanctity through his virtues, his renunciation of wealth and kin, his labor for others in office, and the hope of ecclesiastical commemoration over pagan monuments; it argues against those who measure merit by miracle-novelty and against any who might judge its accounts invented.
b.s: His Vita Odilonis is the principal early witness to Odilo of Cluny and to eleventh-century Cluniac ideals of monastic sanctity, prayer for the dead, and commemoration.

w: Against Book II of Saint Augustine's On Marriage
Book on the good of constancy
Interpretation of the treatise of Rufianus

b.bio: Julian of Eclanum was a fifth-century Italian bishop, son of the bishop Memorius, who succeeded his father in the see of Eclanum near Benevento around 417 under Pope Innocent I. Sources differ on his birth year (Wikipedia and the Catholic Encyclopedia give about 386; Britannica and Encyclopedia.com give 380) and his death date (Catholic Encyclopedia: 454 in Sicily; Britannica and Encyclopedia.com: c. 455 in Sicily). He refused to subscribe to Pope Zosimus's Epistola tractoria of 418 condemning Pelagius and Celestius, was deposed and banished from Italy in 421, and spent his exile writing against Augustine of Hippo. The works held here — the four books to Turbantius, the letter to Zosimus, and treatises on marriage, love, faith, and constancy — belong to that polemical campaign.
b.s: He is described by multiple sources as the most learned/intellectual leader of the Pelagian party, and Augustine answered him in three different works; the volumes here are his own side of that controversy.

b.bio: Julian Pomerius was a priest of Moorish (North African) descent who fled the Vandal conquest of Mauretania for Gaul towards the end of the fifth century. At Arles he was renowned in rhetoric and grammar, numbered Ennodius and Ruricius among his friends, and taught Caesarius of Arles, through whom Augustine's teaching passed into Gallic church life. Of five treatises attributed to him only one survives, De vita contemplativa, held here from PL 59. The excerpted pages argue that God cannot be seen in this mortal life, that the vision of God belongs to the future life alone, that knowledge without charity puffs up while charity edifies, that inquiry exercises the mind even without finding, and that true theology ascribes its insight to God's illumination — against the philosophers.
b.s: His De vita contemplativa is described by Suelzer as the oldest surviving pastoral instruction in the West and a principal channel of Augustinian thought to sixth-century Gaul.

w: Exposition on the Day of Easter and the Month

b.bio: Quintus Julius Hilarianus, a Roman African chronographer and computist, is known only through two treatises completed in 397. His writings suggest he was a monk. He has sometimes been identified with the bishop Hilarianus at the Council of Carthage in 411, but this is uncertain, and he may even have been a Donatist. The Expositum de die Paschae et mensis, finished on 5 March 397, defends the Latin dating of Easter against the Greeks (in agreement with Pope Victor and Nicaea) and was later used in the Carthaginian Computus of 455. The Chronologia sive Libellus de mundi duratione counts 5,530 years from Creation to the Passion and fixes the world's end at c. 498, when the earth reaches 6,000 years.
b.s: He is one of the last vocal proponents of Latin millenarianism: his Libellus predicts the Second Coming in 498 followed by Christ's thousand-year reign, a view soon classed as heresy, yet the work circulated in medieval chronological manuscript groups.

b.bio: Justinian II, last emperor of the Heraclian dynasty, reigned twice (685–695 and 705–711), was deposed after a popular uprising in 695, had his nose cut off by the usurper Leontios, regained the throne with Bulgarian help in 705, and was killed by mutinous soldiers in 711. He came into conflict with the papacy because he would not accept the supremacy of the Roman see. The work held here under his name is a one-page imperial text asserting that the emperor is guardian of the faith and that conciliar definitions are inviolable; it cites the Sixth Ecumenical Council. The library shelves it among the Latin Fathers, but its author is a Byzantine emperor writing in Greek.
b.s: The single page held here shows the Byzantine imperial claim to guardianship of doctrine, grounded in subscription to conciliar definitions confirmed by the fathers.

b.bio: Jean Labouderie, abbé, born at Chalinargues in Cantal on 13 February 1776, died in Paris on 2 May 1849. Trained first as an advocate, he studied biblical languages at the Collège de France and became vicaire bibliophile at Notre-Dame de Paris from 1811, later grand vicaire of Avignon and canon of Saint-Flour. He was a member of the Société des antiquaires de France (1823–1840), the Académie de Rouen, and the Société asiatique, and also wrote Bible translations in Auvergnat dialects under the name Joan Labodaria. The library's shelf label 'Latin Fathers' is misleading: this is a nineteenth-century French scholar, not a patristic author.
b.s: The single work held here is a short scholarly notice arguing that Moses of Norwich converted as Petrus Alphonsi under King Alfonso, surveying citations from Wolf, Nicolas Antonio, Mariana, Ferreras, Hardt, Rossi and Rodriguez de Castro, and engaging the objections of Rabbis Jacob ben Reuben and Shem Tov ben Isaac ben Shaprut.

b.bio: Johann Martin Lappenberg was born in Hamburg in 1794 and died there in 1865. Trained first in medicine at Edinburgh and then in law, he took a doctorate at Göttingen in 1816. After serving briefly as Hamburg's resident minister at the Prussian court in Berlin (1820), he became keeper of the Hamburg archives in 1823, holding the post until failing eyesight forced his retirement in 1863. He represented Hamburg in the Frankfurt parliament in 1850. His scholarship centered on the early Holy Roman Empire, Anglo-Saxon and Norman England, and the Hanseatic League; his Geschichte von England (1834–1837) remains his best-known work.
b.s: He is not a Latin Father but a modern critical historian: the five-page 'Notice on Thietmar' held here is his editorial apparatus introducing the chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg in Migne's Patrologia Latina 139.

w: Dissertations on the Life and Writings of Saint Paulinus

b.bio: Jean-Baptiste Le Brun, called Desmarettes, was born at Rouen around 1651, son of the bookseller Bonaventure Le Brun, who was condemned to the galleys for printing works in favor of Port-Royal. His mother took refuge at Port-Royal de Paris with her two sons, who were raised in the Port-Royal orbit; Jean-Baptiste kept close ties to the abbey of Port-Royal des Champs into the 1680s. He is not the painter Jean-Baptiste-Pierre Lebrun (1748–1813), husband of Élisabeth Vigée-Lebrun; that homonym is disregarded here.
b.s: The work held here is his set of dissertations on the life and writings of Saint Paulinus, a critical historical apparatus that dates Paulinus's withdrawal to Spain (390), ordination as presbyter at Barcelona (393), and individual letters, arguing against Baronius, Sacchinus, Rosweyde, Francis Juret, and the common published editions on points such as the separate status of the epistle to Licentius and an ancient lacuna in epistle nine.

b.bio: Jean Lebeuf was a French historian and antiquary, born at Auxerre in March 1687 (sources differ on whether 6 or 7 March) to a father who served as receveur des consignations; he studied at Auxerre and at the Collège Sainte-Barbe in Paris, and died in Paris on 10 April 1760. He mastered practically every branch of medieval learning, traveled France examining monuments and libraries, published dissertations on the civil and ecclesiastical history of Paris and an Histoire de la ville et de tout le diocèse de Paris, and won prizes from the Académie de Soissons and the Académie des Inscriptions in 1740, entering that body the same year. He was named honorary canon of Auxerre cathedral. The work held here is his two-page preface to a volume of the Patrologia Latina (PL 20), reflecting his editorial work on patristic texts.
b.s: Lebeuf matters to readers of this library as the learned eighteenth-century editor whose preface introduces the patristic material printed in PL 20.

b.bio: No source gives dates, birthplace, office, or order for this medieval writer. the surviving records describe other men of similar name — Jean Lepage (b. 1946), a modern French author and museum administrator, and Jean-Denis Lepage (b. 1952), a modern historian-illustrator — none of whom matches the author of a Latin Life of Philip of Harveng printed in PL 203, so they cannot be used for this note. What is known comes from the work itself as recorded in the library record: he wrote a Life of Philip of Harveng, cites Philip most frequently, and argues against certain malicious religious of his own order.
b.s: His Life of Philip of Harveng is the record held here: it asserts that grace, more powerful than nature, converts man, and treats tribulation as working patience and hope.

b.bio: None of The surviving records identifies a Johannes Lindnerus connected to this work. They describe two different men named Lindner: Johannes Lindner (c. 1450–c. 1530), a Dominican at Pirna and opponent of the Reformation, and Johann Gottlieb Lindner (1726–1811), a Saxon schoolmaster and historian who also wrote as 'Lindnerus'. Neither matches a Latin patristic author. The library's single item under this name is a four-page logical analysis of the dialogue Octavius, arguing for God's existence, creation, providence, and unity against the pagan Caecilius — that is, an analytical treatment of Minucius Felix's text, not an independent patristic work.
b.s: The work held here matters as a compact logical breakdown of Minucius Felix's Octavius, tracing its proofs for God, creation, and providence against Caecilius.

w: Addition to the Life of St. Amandus
Dissertation on Eucharistic Bread, Unleavened and Leavened
Notice on the short work of Ildefonsus
On the Deeds of Gregory VII
Preface to the Life of St. Gregory VII
Preliminary Observations on the Life of St. Boniface
Supplement to the Book of the Daily Office of the Roman Pontiffs

b.bio: Born at Saint-Pierremont in Champagne on 23 November 1632 to Estienne Mabillon and Jeanne Guérin. He studied at the Collège des Bons Enfants at Reims, entered the diocesan seminary in 1650, then left it and became a monk at the Maurist abbey of Saint-Rémi, Reims, in 1653. Ordained priest at Corbie in 1660, he moved in 1664 to Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, the headquarters of the Maurist scholars. There he edited patristic and liturgical texts, wrote historical eulogies of Benedictine abbots such as Maiolus and Odilo, and composed De re diplomatica, which founded palaeography and diplomatics. He died in Paris on 27 December 1707.
b.s: The works held here are his editions, prolegomena, dissertations, and historical eulogies: critical scholarship that dated manuscripts, defended Gallican liturgy and leavened Eucharistic bread against Dallaeus, Sirmond, Baronius, and the Greeks, and established saints' intercession and abbatial election from sources.

b.bio: Spanish Jesuit born in April 1536 at Talavera de la Reina, near Toledo; entered the Society of Jesus on 1 January 1554 and taught theology in Rome (from 1561), Sicily, and Paris (1569–1574) before returning to Spain in 1574 owing to ill health, where he lived and wrote at the Jesuits' house in Toledo until his death there on 16 February 1624. He is chiefly remembered as the historian of Spain, author of Historiae de rebus Hispaniae (Toledo, 1592), later extended to the accession of Philip IV, and as the controversialist of De rege et regis institutione (1598), whose treatment of tyrannicide made him one of the most maligned members of his order.
b.s: The items held here under his name are not his histories but his testimony on the Chronicle attributed to Isidore of Pacensis: he argues that Isidore wrote it, while holding that the chronicle retains its great authority regardless of who composed it, citing Vasaeus, Ambrosius Morales, and Rodericus, prelate of Toledo.

b.bio: Dom Jacques Martin (Jacques de Martin), born at Fanjeaux on 11 May 1684 and died in Paris on 5 September 1751, was a Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint-Maur. Son of a lawyer, he studied at Toulouse, entered the Maurist congregation in 1709, taught humanities at Sorèze, and moved to Paris in 1727. He wrote chiefly on the history of Gaul and the religion of the Celtes, notably La Religion des Gaulois (Paris, 1727), which argued that Gallic religion derived from that of the patriarchs. A separate Jacques Martin (1794–1874), a Protestant preacher of Geneva, is a different man and not this author. The pieces held here are his editorial contributions—preface and admonitions—to the Migne edition of Augustine's letters in PL 33.
b.s: The works held here are a Maurist scholar's preface and textual admonitions accompanying Augustine's letters in PL 33, guiding readers through problems in those epistles.

b.bio: Joseph Meglinger, baptized Karl Jost, was born in Lucerne on 10 November 1634, son of the painter Kaspar Meglinger. He entered Wettingen Abbey under Abbot Bernhard Keller and professed as frater Joseph on 12 June 1655; ordained priest on 21 December 1658, he served as abbatial secretary (1665–1672), subprior (1666–1668), pastor of Wettingen (1668–1669), confessor at Kalchrain (1672–1676), and was made Notarius Apostolicus on 23 July 1670. In May 1667 Abbot Gerhard Bürgisser sent him as delegate to the General Chapter at Cîteaux; the journey is the subject of his Descriptio itineris Cisterciensis (Lucerne, 1667), dedicated to General Vicar Edmund Schnyder of St. Urban. He also ran the abbey press and wrote on geometry and surveying.
b.s: His Descriptio itineris Cisterciensis is a first-hand narrative of a delegate's journey to the 1667 General Chapter, defending Cistercian origins and unity under one head against 'sectaries' and Calvinist critics while celebrating Bernard and the order's history.

b.t: French Catholic theologian and book editor
b.bio: Jacques Merlin was born at Saint-Victurnien in Limousin around 1480, took his doctorate in theology at the College of Navarre in 1499, and taught divinity to the chapter of Saint-Étienne de Limoges before moving to Paris, where he became curate of Montmartre, resident canon of Notre-Dame, and in 1525 its chief penitentiary. He edited Origen's works (1511–12) with an Apologie d'Origene that drew condemnation from the Paris Faculty under Noel Beda, and he compiled a pioneering printed collection of church councils, the Quatuor concilia generalia (1524). In 1527 Francis I imprisoned him for preaching against courtiers suspected of sympathy with reform; released after two years, he returned to Paris by 1530 as grand-vicar to the bishop.
b.s: The library holds only a single-page epistle under his name, which cites Isidore and the Council of Basel — consistent with his editorial interest in conciliar texts rather than any independent theological system.

b.bio: Jean Dumoulin (Joannes Molinaeus), born in Ghent in 1525 and died September 29, 1575, studied and taught at Louvain, where King Philip II appointed him to the chair of Canon Law on August 9, 1557; he became rector of the university a year later. He opposed subjecting certain abbeys to new bishoprics, went to Rome in 1573 seeking their suppression, returned unsuccessful, and was summoned before the bishops' council at Mechelen; his orthodoxy was questioned over these events and his writings, and it is possible he lost his mind, entered seclusion, and starved himself to death. He published an edition of Ivo of Chartres's Decretum at Louvain in 1562, judging it better arranged than Gratian.
b.s: The library holds his Letter to Bernard of Fresneda, which argues that restoration of the church lies in reviving ancient canon law rather than new councils, ranks Ivo of Chartres above Gratian as the best canonistic authority, argues that punishments have failed to extinguish heresy, and answers the heretics of his own time.

w: Inquiry into the Date of the Apologeticum

b.bio: Johann Lorenz von Mosheim was born at Lübeck on 9 October 1693 or 1694 (sources differ) and died at Göttingen on 9 September 1755. After studies at Kiel, where he took his master's degree in 1718 and became assessor in the philosophical faculty in 1719, he was called as professor ordinarius to Helmstedt in 1723. He became abbot of Marienthal in 1726 and of Michaelstein the next year, helped frame the statutes of the new University of Göttingen, and in 1747 was made its chancellor. His Institutiones Historiae Ecclesiasticae (1726) founded what Britannica calls the pragmatic school of church history, insisting on critical treatment of sources.
b.s: The work held here is a chronological dissertation arguing that Tertullian's Apologeticum was written in 198 under Septimius Severus, against the martyr chronologies of Dodwell, Allix, Pagius, and Baronius.

w: Preface to the Cycles of Cyril and others

b.bio: Johannes Noviomagus is the Latin name of Jan van Bronckhorst, born at Nijmegen in 1494 and died at Cologne in 1570. He taught philosophy at the Collegium Montanum in Cologne from about 1539, then mathematics at Rostock from 1542 (rector there 1543–44), and was rector of the Latin school at Deventer in 1546. He translated Ptolemy's Geography into Latin and published an edition of the Almagest star catalogue with celestial maps after Dürer (Cologne 1537), besides editing scholia on Georgius Trapezuntius and Bede. A second Johannes Noviomagus, a Latin teacher at the same Cologne gymnasium dated c. 1509–1569, appears in cartographic literature; sources disagree over whether these are one man or two.
b.s: The work held here is his preface to restored Easter cycles, arguing that corrupted cycles were corrected as of 1595, that eighty-four-year Easter cycles reduce to twenty-eight great cycles, and that the great cycle repeats everything except indictions and dominical letters — computistical material in the tradition of Bede, whom he cites.

b.bio: Johann Conrad von Orelli was a Swiss Protestant theologian and classical philologist of Zürich. Born there on 22 August 1770, he studied theology in the city, was ordained in 1792, and taught at the Carolinum as professor of church history (from 1794) and ethics (from 1796), serving also as its rector in 1815–1816; he was deacon at the Fraumünster from 1796 and became pastor of the Dominicans' church and canon of the Grossmünster chapter in 1810. He edited Greek and Latin texts, including Sallust's De deo mundi (Peri theōn kai kosmu), the Opuscula Graecorum veterum sententiosa et moralia, and an edition of Arnobius.
b.s: The work held here is his appendix to the disputations prefacing his edition of Arnobius, where he assesses Arnobius against Tertullian, Origen, Jerome, Ambrose, and Chrysostom, traces the manuscript tradition to a single Paris codex (copied by the Flacius-Petraeus codex), and credits Leibniz with clarifying the doctrine of the best world.

w: Life and Letters of John Cirita

b.bio: The name Joannes Pepermanus as it appears here does not belong to the seventeenth-century Brussels printer Jan Pepermans (active 1620–1633/1635), who is sometimes Latinized as Joannes Pepermannus but published courtly and Habsburg materials as official printer of the city of Brussels; that man is a homonym and is set aside. The work held under this name is a five-page life and letters of John Cirita, a hermit whose conversion, struggle against demonic temptation of lust, and foundation of a monastery are narrated there. The text cites an old manuscript book of the monastery of St. Christopher and names John Marquez among its witnesses.
b.s: The single work held here is a brief hagiographical history of John Cirita, arguing that divine providence calls sinners to conversion through grace and that grace gives victory over demonic temptation of lust (defeated by bodily mortification), and recording John the Baptist's command to Bernard to found a Spanish monastery licensed by princely charter.

b.bio: Juan Bautista Pérez Rubert was born in Valencia around 1537 (Catholic-Hierarchy gives 1534) and died there in 1597 (sources give November or December). Educated at the University of Valencia in theology, canon law, Hebrew, Greek and Arabic, he taught Hebrew there before gaining the patronage of Archbishop Martín Pérez de Ayala and then Cardinal Gaspar de Quiroga, under whom he worked on the collection of Spanish councils commissioned by Gregory XIII. He served as canon and librarian at Toledo cathedral, acted as secretary at the last Council of Toledo, and was presented by Philip II to the see of Segorbe in 1591. He corrected Isidore of Seville's Historia de los godos, vándalos y suevos and exposed the forged chronicles attributed to Dextro and Máximo.
b.s: The work held here, the Admonition printed in PL 96, belongs to his editorial and critical work on the texts of the Visigothic-era Spanish church, notably Isidore and Ildefonsus.

w: Analytical index to the works of Garnerius
Eulogy on the excellence and utility of this work

b.bio: This is not the seventeenth-century astronomer Jean Picard (1620–1682) described in most reference sources; the works held here belong to a different man of the same name, a French humanist born at Beauvais in the sixteenth century who died in 1617. He was a regular canon of St. Victor in Paris and edited patristic and medieval texts, including Guillaume de Neubourg's chronicle (Paris, 1610) and the OEuvres de St. Bernard (Paris, 1615). The pieces in this volume are his editorial apparatus for Garnerius's eleventh-century anthology of passages from Gregory the Great: a preface, address to the reader, dedicatory letter, eulogy, and analytical index.
b.s: His prefatory material and index frame Garnerius's florilegium of Gregory as an indispensable handbook for students and ecclesiastics, while arguing against Sixtus of Siena and Arnold Wion on questions of attribution and textual order.

w: Notes on the collections of Smaragdus

b.bio: Jean-Baptiste-François Pitra, born at Champforgeuil on 1 August 1812, was a French Benedictine who entered the Abbey of Solesmes in 1842 and worked with Abbé Migne on the Patrologia latina and Patrologia graeca. He deciphered the Inscription of Autun in 1839, published the Spicilegium Solesmense, was made cardinal in 1863, and served as librarian of the Vatican Library from 1869. He died in Rome on 9 February 1889. The work held here is his editorial apparatus for volume 102 of Migne's Patrologia latina: notes on Smaragdus's collections of patristic sayings, drawing on twenty patristic authors as sources and discussing how Carolingian homiliaries served the Roman liturgy in Gaul, including identifying a Bologna codex as the Saint-Bertin homiliary of Abbot John.
b.s: Pitra edited and annotated the patristic florilegia printed in PL 102, so readers of Smaragdus in this library are reading Pitra's identification of the excerpted authors and their sources.

w: Observations on the book concerning ecclesiastical offices

b.bio: the surviving records describe two different men named Jean Prévost — a Jesuit Thomist commentator (1570–1634) and a twentieth-century French writer and Resistance fighter (1901–1944) — neither of whom matches the works held here. The library record alone identifies this Jean Prévost as a scholar of medieval liturgy whose editorial apparatus appears in PL 147: observations on the book concerning ecclesiastical offices (the De officio ecclesiastico associated with John of Rouen) and an index to John of Rouen.
b.s: His notes defend the ancient usage of the holy church of Rouen against William Durand and more recent scribes/editors, tracing the apostolic origin of the tonsure to St Peter and surveying Amalarius, Alcuin, John Beleth, Isidore, and the Micrologus on night reading and the psalms.

b.bio: The library holds a single page under this name: a letter on variant readings printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 12. None of the surviving records describe an author named Joannes Raverdy, and they concern other figures entirely — Molanus, John of Jandun, Bunderius, Johannes Teutonicus — so nothing can be asserted here about his life, dates, or offices. The attribution within PL 12 suggests the piece belongs to the editorial apparatus or correspondence surrounding the patristic texts in that volume rather than to any of those men.
b.s: His sole work here is a one-page letter on variant readings in PL 12, i.e., textual notes attached to the corpus printed in that volume.

b.bio: None of the surviving records describes this Jean Robert. They record instead a sixteenth-century auxiliary bishop of Nantes, a modern French classicist (Jean-Noël Robert), the Jesuit controversialist Jean Roberti (1569–1651), and the scholar Jean-Robert Armogathe — different men, none connected to Echternach, so none may be used for this author. What can be said comes from the library record alone: this author wrote a short Life of Thiofrid, abbot of Echternach, together with dedication forewords addressed to readers. In the Life he defends Thiofrid's true name against those who derive 'Vernatus' from the dedication verse, arguing it is a corruption of 'verna tuus'; he cites Gregory VII, Bernard, Benedict, Willibrord, Bertelius, and annotations by Echternach religious.
b.s: His works here form the hagiographical apparatus to Thiofrid of Echternach in PL 157: a brief vita defending the abbot's name and character, not a major theological treatise.

b.bio: Julianus Martianus Rota was a Venetian scholar of the sixteenth century whose recorded activity is editorial rather than authorial. He is credited with editions of Boethius's De consolatione philosophiae and with the 1570 Basel folio Opera omnia issued by the Henricpetrina press, which included Johann Murmellius's commentary on the Consolation, Rudolph Agricola's enarrationes, Gilbert de la Porrée's commentaries on De trinitate, and Glareanus's augmented demonstrations of Boethius's Arithmetic and Music. The library holds only the dedicatory letter prefixed to that edition.
b.s: The single page held here is Rota's dedication of his 1570 Boethius edition; it surveys Boethius's theological works, asserting they were written before exile (the christological treatise in youth) and left incomplete at death, and defends their Chalcedonian Christology against Nestorius, Eutyches, and the Acephali.

b.bio: Jules, Baron de Saint-Genois (22 March 1813, Sint-Kwintens-Lennik – 10 September 1867, Ghent) was a Belgian historian, librarian and professor at the University of Ghent. He served as provincial archivist of East Flanders from 1836, was the first president of the Willemsfonds, and president of the editorial committee of the Biographie Nationale de Belgique at the Académie royale de Belgique. A doctor of law trained at Ghent, he published historical novels in French and Dutch alongside archival inventories and a catalogue of the Ghent university manuscripts. He was not a church father or medieval author; the library holds only his introductory notice to the Liber Floridus printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina.
b.s: The single work held here is his seven-page notice on the Liber Floridus of Lambert of Saint-Omer (PL 163), placing this modern scholar's edition apparatus beside the twelfth-century encyclopedist it describes.

b.bio: Giovanni Maria Salvioni was a Roman printer, not a theologian. Son of Giovan Michele and Pelagia Reali, he first worked in his father's metallurgical shop, then opened a printing business near Campo de' Fiori after his father's death in 1704. A gift of a printed Life of St Francis to Clement XI won him management of the Stamperia Vaticana from 1715; he was formally named papal printer in 1717, with privileges renewed by Benedict XIII and extended to his sons. By his death in 1755 the press had produced roughly 500 titles.
b.s: The single page held here is a dedication letter prefacing an edition of the Liber Pontificalis, arguing that its brief pontifical lives serve historical truth and citing Baronius, Eusebius, Surius, Binius, Holstenius and other editors; Salvioni matters as the printer-publisher behind major Roman editions, including Lancisi's De motu cordis et aneurysmatibus (1728).

b.bio: Johann Salomo Semler was born at Saalfeld in Saxe-Saalfeld on 18 December 1725 and died at Halle on 14 March 1791. A disciple of S. J. Baumgarten at Halle, he became professor of theology there in 1752 and led the theological faculty after Baumgarten's death in 1757. He is remembered as a pioneer of historical-critical study of Scripture and church documents, an approach that drew strong opposition. The work held here under his name is a set of philological notes on the Latin Fathers' account of letters — Irenaeus on corrupted Hebrew letterforms, Augustine against a late invention of the alphabet, Ezekiel's thau as sign or letter, Palamedes' three Greek letters — correcting readings in Isidore against Servius, Victorinus, Gothofredus, Turnebus, and Schukford.
b.s: The notes here show the textual critic applying philological method to patristic claims about alphabets and scriptural signs, weighing Isidore's text against grammarians like Priscian, Diomedes, and Festus.

b.bio: Johannes Sichardus was born in Tauberbischofsheim around 1499 and died in Tübingen on 9 September 1552. A humanist and jurist, he taught rhetoric at Basel from 1524 to 1530, lecturing on Cicero and Quintilian and later on law, and was involved in the authorship of more than twenty books for Basel printers including Andreas Cratander and Adam Petri. He ended his career as professor of law at Tübingen. The epistle held here is his prefatory letter to his edition of Chromatius of Aquileia, in which he defends the value of that father's writings on baptism against modern controversialists.
b.s: Sichard matters here as the editor who recovered Chromatius of Aquileia for sixteenth-century readers; his letter argues that the ancient fathers settle modern baptism controversies and cites Albinus to confirm Chromatius as Jerome's correspondent.

w: Index to the works of Prosper
Letter on the Edition of Saint Valerian
Letter to the Carthusians of Mont-Dieu

b.bio: Jacques Sirmond, born at Riom in Auvergne on 12 October 1559, entered the Society of Jesus in 1576 and taught classical languages in Paris before serving for sixteen years in Rome as secretary to the Jesuit general Claudio Acquaviva. He returned to Paris in 1608 and became confessor to Louis XIII in 1637. His career was spent editing Greek and Latin Christian writers — Sidonius Apollinaris, Ennodius, Hincmar, Hrabanus Maurus, Theodulf of Orléans — and publishing the capitularies of Charles the Bald and the ancient councils of France. The works held under his name here are not those editions themselves but his prefatory matter, admonitions, and dissertations attached to them: notes on predestination and grace, defenses of Prosper and Hincmar against predestinarian readings, and legal-formula material.
b.s: The volumes here preserve Sirmond's editorial apparatus — prefaces, admonitions, and dissertations on grace, free will, and predestination — through which seventeenth-century readers received the anti-predestinarian tradition of Prosper, Hincmar, and the councils of ancient France.

w: Annotations on the Works of Bede

b.bio: John Smith (1659–1715) — John Smith was born at Lowther, Westmorland on 10 November 1659, one of eleven brothers. He studied at St John's College, Cambridge (B.A. 1677, M.A. 1681), was ordained by Archbishop Sterne, and became a minor canon of Durham Cathedral in 1682, later chaplain to Lord Lansdown at Madrid (1686–89). Bishop Nathaniel Crew collated him to Gateshead rectory in 1695 and to a prebendal stall at Durham; he became D.D. at Cambridge in 1696 and treasurer of Durham in 1699, adding the rectory of Bishop-Wearmouth in 1704. His health failed from 1713 and he died in 1715.
b.s: He is remembered for his edition of Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum; the works held here are his annotations on Bede's texts, in which he defends Bede against the criticisms of Oxford scholars and Stillingfleet, drawing on Camden, Nennius, Gildas, Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory of Tours.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies this Jean-Baptiste Soller. The sources given describe different seventeenth-century Frenchmen bearing similar names: Jean-Baptiste Cotelier (born December 1629 at Nîmes, died 19 August 1686 at Paris), patristic scholar of the Sorbonne and Collège Royal; Jean-Baptiste de Santeul (1630–1697), canon of St. Victor and Latin poet; and Jean-Baptiste Saint-Jure (1588–1657), Jesuit spiritual writer. None is credited with the works held here, so none can be asserted as this author. What the library holds under this name is front matter to a volume of hagiographical material in PL 123: a Preface, a one-page Prolegomena treating theological method, and a Protestation.
b.s: The works here are preliminary matter for an edition of saints' acts, arguing that hagiographical commentaries are mere human history and that papal constitutions — Urban VIII's are cited — govern how such acts may be treated.

b.bio: Jean-Baptiste Souchet (Joannes Baptista Souchetus), born and died at Chartres (baptized 4 February 1589, died 9 April 1654), was a French cleric and historian. A doctor of theology of the Sorbonne, he served as notary (1615), curé of Abondant (1618), secretary to the chapter of Notre-Dame, and canon of Chartres cathedral from 1632. He corresponded with the Maurist Luc d'Achery (letters of 3 August 1648 and 18 December 1651) and edited works connected with Ivo of Chartres. His chief labor, an Histoire du diocèse et de la ville de Chartres, remained in manuscript until its publication in four volumes in 1866–1868 (including his Veritatis defensio). The Observations printed in PL 162 are his critical annotations on the letters of Ivo of Chartres.
b.s: His Observations in PL 162 correct Baronius on points touching Ivo of Chartres — dating letters to 1090, c. 1092, and 1094/1095, and clarifying customs such as monastic election of rules and the terminology of altars and tithes — drawing heavily on Orderic Vitalis.

b.bio: No source in this record identifies a Johannes Spanheim. the surviving records describe three seventeenth-century Calvinists named Spanheim: Friedrich the Elder (1600–1649), professor of theology at Leiden and defender of predestination against Amyraldism; his son Friedrich the Younger (1632–1701), professor at Heidelberg and Leiden; and Ezechiel (1629–1710), diplomat and antiquary. None is a Johannes, none belongs to the Latin Fathers, and none matches the work held here. The name as printed in Migne's PL 167 cannot be confirmed against these sources.
b.s: The single page held under this name treats prayer joined to doctrine as exceeding contemplation alone, double honor for those presiding well in doctrine, reform restoring ancient observance, love of God as operative rather than idle, and zeal for souls above all sacrifices, citing Rupert and Gerlac.

b.bio: Jerónimo Zurita y Castro, born in Zaragoza on 4 December 1512, studied at Alcalá de Henares and served Charles V and Philip II in a succession of offices, including secretary to the council of the Inquisition (from 1566), before being appointed official chronicler of the kingdom of Aragon in 1548. He resigned his posts on 21 January 1571 to devote himself to his Anales de la Corona de Aragón, the first part of which appeared in 1562 and the last volume of which was printed at Zaragoza on 22 April 1580; he died in 1580 (sources differ between 31 October and 3 November). He is regarded as the founder of modern historical scholarship in Spain. He is not a church father; the library's 'Latin Fathers' shelf label appears to be a misplacement.
b.s: The single page held here is a letter to Antonio Agustín preserved in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 149); Zurita matters as the first Spanish historian to work from archival sources rather than legend.

b.bio:
J. Szlachtowski (1816–1871) — Jan Kanty Szlachtowski, born 30 October 1816 in Lwów and died 13 November 1871, was professor of Polish language and literature at the University of Lwów and director of the Zakład Narodowy im. Ossolińskich, writing under initials including J.S., J.Szl., and Wydawca. The library holds under his name only a two-page 'Prolegomena' printed in Patrologia Latina vol. 160, which fits his work as an editor of patristic and medieval texts rather than any of the other figures these sources describe. Marcin Szlachciński (1511/1512–1600), Jagiellonian professor and translator; Szymon Starowolski (1588–1656), writer and historian; and Antoni Władysław Szlagowski (1864–1956), Warsaw biblical scholar, are different men and are not treated here.

Rudolf Koepke (1813–1870) — Ernst Rudolf Anastasius Köpke was a German historian born in Königsberg. He studied theology in Berlin from 1832 before turning to history under Leopold von Ranke, becoming an early member of the Ranke school alongside Georg Waitz, Wilhelm von Giesebrecht, and Siegfried Hirsch. He taught at the Joachimsthal Gymnasium in Berlin (1838–1842), worked with the Monumenta Germaniae Historica, taught history at the Berlin Kriegsakademie (1850–1867), and received the title of associate professor in 1856. He wrote a two-volume biography of Ludwig Tieck, studies of Widukind of Corvey and Hrotsvitha of Gandersheim, and co-founded the Jahrbücher der Deutschen Geschichte.
b.s: His 'Prolegomena' in PL 160 is editorial front matter for that volume of Migne's series; readers should treat it as a nineteenth-century scholar's introduction, not a patristic text.

b.bio: Jean du Tillet was a French Catholic bishop and manuscript collector, brother of the archivist Jean du Tillet, sieur de La Bussière; the two collaborated in scholarship. He was appointed bishop of Saint-Brieuc in 1553 and became bishop of Meaux in 1564. A Gallican, he attended the Council of Trent, encouraged Gentian Hervet's Latin translation of Photius' Syntagma with Balsamon's commentary, and in 1553 obtained in Rome a Hebrew version of Matthew's Gospel. In 1549 he first published the Libri Carolini from a manuscript he owned. Sources disagree on his death date: Wikipedia gives 18 December 1570, the Cyclopedia gives 19 November 1570.
b.s: The works held here are his prefatory and dedicatory matter for his 1568 edition of Lucifer of Cagliari's works against Emperor Constantius II, defending Lucifer's orthodoxy against those who would number the Luciferians among heretics or posit two Lucifers, and arguing that public disputation with heretics is sinful — a polemic aimed at proponents of the Colloquy of Poissy amid France's religious crisis.

b.bio: The library holds only two short prefatory pieces under this name: a dedicatory letter and an address 'To the reader' introducing William of Apulia's poem on Robert Guiscard, which the preface presents as newly discovered. The preface argues that Christian poetry must reject pagan fable for truth, that eyewitness contemporaneity grounds a historian's authority, that the Normans migrated for glory rather than exile, and that the scarcity of writers on Norman deeds justifies publication; it cites Horace, Virgil, 'Maeonides', and the Platonic polity, and is addressed to a Norman patron of noble lineage. None of The surviving records describes this person; they cover Johannes Hentenius, Susenbrotus, Johannes Teutonicus, and Torrentius, whose careers do not match these works.
b.s: These pages are the prefatory apparatus by which William of Apulia's Gesta Roberti Wiscardi was presented to readers in this edition, framing its claims of eyewitness authority and Christian historiography against classical fable.

b.bio: A Flemish cleric recorded in the Ostend city archive as dean of the decanate of Oudenburg from 1656 to 1661 and canon of Sint-Donaas (St. Donatian) in Bruges; the biographical entry cites H. Vansteenkiste's study of church life in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Ostend. No birth or death dates are given in the sources. Other authors named Jean-Baptiste in the sources — the poet Santeul, the Jesuit Saint-Jure, the patristic scholar Cotelier — are different men and are not this author.
b.s: The library holds a single work under his name, a Censure printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 210), which cites Alanus Magnus de Insulis (Alan of Lille) as its most-cited authority.

b.bio:
Vendemoere, Joseph (unknown) — No surviving record identifies an author named Joseph Vendemoere. The name does not match Matthew of Vendôme (12th-century poet), Geoffrey of Vendôme (c. 1065/70–1132, abbot and cardinal), Joseph de Jouvancy (1643–1719, Jesuit historian), or Joseph Vendryes (1875–1960, Celticist), though the surname suggests some connection to Vendôme. The library holds under this name only a nineteen-page historical notice printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 89. Whether the notice is by this Joseph or concerns him cannot be determined from the record.

Vanhecke, Joseph (1795–1874) — Joseph Vanhecke (printed in sources as Joseph Van Hecke) was born in 1795 at Bruges. He entered the Jesuits in 1814 and taught canon law at Freiburg in Switzerland and in Belgium. In 1837 he moved to Brussels to work on the continuation of the Acta Sanctorum, the Bollandist project. He wrote studies of Johannes Capistranus and of Ignatius, patriarch of Constantinople. He died July 27, 1874. A homonym must be set aside: Englebert Vincent Joseph Vanhecke (1740–1809), a church musician of the Austrian Netherlands recorded in the MUSEFREM database, is a different man.
b.s: The single item held is a brief historical notice in PL 89; its value to readers cannot be assessed beyond its presence in that volume, as no source describes it.

b.bio: The sources do not establish who this John of Nicaea was. A prosopographical search (source:1) found no entry for him in the Prosopography of the Byzantine World or the Prosopographie der mittelbyzantinischen Zeit, and could only suggest he belongs somewhere between the 9th and the 12th century, after the coverage of the Clavis Patrum Graecorum ends with John Damascene. The other sources describe different men: a 20th-century Finnish metropolitan who took Nicaea as a titular see (source:2), and John Chrysostom (sources:3-4); neither is this author. What can be said comes from the library record: the single work held here is a short polemical and exegetical piece on Christology, Scripture, sin, the church, grace, and sacraments, written against Gretser, Leo Allatius, the Armenians, Isaac the Catholicos, and a Greek editor, citing Paul, Chrysostom, James, Josephus, Luke, David, Photius, and Julius.
b.s: His one short work in PG 96 is a Byzantine polemical-exegetical text defending Christology and sacramental teaching against Latin controversialists (Gretser, Allatius) and eastern opponents such as the Armenians and Isaac the Catholicos.

b.bio: Johannes de Euboea, a Greek author placed by Biblissima between 601 and 799, is described as a monk and presbyter, or possibly bishop, of Euboea ('JOANNES, Euboeæ monachus et presbyter, vel episcopus'). The Clavis (CPG 8135–8138) attributes to him a Homilia in conceptionem Deiparae, a Homilia in Lazarum, a Homilia in sanctos Innocentes, and a Passio S. Parasceuae. The library holds his homily on the Conception of the Mother of God (PG 96), an exegetical work arguing from Isaiah, Psalm 45, and 1 Kings that Mary was immaculate — called 'heaven' rather than 'earthly' because she did not share the corrupted condition of other children of Adam — and recounting her offering in the temple at age three. He should not be confused with the later 16th-century saint David of Euboea.
b.s: His homily on Mary's conception is an early Byzantine text arguing for her immaculate condition on exegetical grounds, and is the work held here.

b.bio: John Kalekas was born about 1282 in Aprus (Apros), Thrace, married with a son and daughter, and ordained a priest. Through the patronage of John Kantakouzenos he rose to the patriarchate of Constantinople in February 1334, succeeding Isaias I (and succeeded by Isidore I). He led the anti-hesychast opposition to Gregory Palamas, participating in the synod proceedings of 1341, and his patriarchate ended on 2 February 1347, coinciding with Kantakouzenos's victory in the Byzantine civil war of 1341–1347, on whose regency side he had fought. He died in Constantinople on 29 December 1347. The single short text held here under his name is an ascension homily printed in Migne's PG 150: it treats Christology, sin, and sanctification, asserting that only the incarnate Son ascended to the highest heaven by his own innate power, that ecstatic ascent occurs only by God's command, and that Jacob's ladder vision concerns a lower heaven. The piece argues against Jacob Gretser's attribution of this Philotheus homily, maintaining it is Caleca's.
b.s: He matters chiefly as the patriarchal leader of the anti-hesychast opposition to Gregory Palamas; the work here is a brief ascension homily transmitted under his name, engaged with Jacob Gretser's attribution of it to Philotheus.

b.bio: John Kananos (John Cananus) was a Byzantine Greek historian active in the first half of the fifteenth century. He wrote an eyewitness account of the failed Ottoman siege of Constantinople under Murad II in 1422, attributing the city's survival to the intervention of the Mother of God, whom he says even the Ottomans saw on the ramparts on 24 August. He wrote in vernacular Greek for ordinary readers rather than scholars, apologizing for his deficient education, and his account is precise in chronology and valuable for its descriptions of Ottoman siegecraft and Byzantine defences.
b.s: His account of the 1422 siege is a vivid eyewitness narrative combining military history with religious polemic against the Turks and their emir Mersaita, and it defends Constantinople's standing as Rome's equal rather than its colony.

b.bio: John, called Anagnostes ('lector'), was a Greek historian of the fifteenth century and a native of Thessalonica. He was present at the Ottoman sack of his city on 29 March 1430 under Murad II; after the fall he left Thessalonica but was induced to return by the conqueror's promises, and two years later Murad deprived him of all his property. He wrote an eyewitness account of the storming of the city with an accompanying prose monody lamenting its fall, composed after 1433.
b.s: His Account of the Last Capture of Thessalonica is a primary eyewitness narrative of the Ottoman conquest of 1430, reading the calamity as divine punishment for sin.
